speechtext: This affords me an opportunity to say that there is some delay in getting the resolutions before committee of ways and means, by reason of a cable communication with Australia. Several items of the tariff wild be modified in the light of a trade agreement we propose to make with that dominion, an'd we have been asked not to proceed with these matters until we receive the original of the trade agreement executed in Australia. It should not have been; it was not in correct form. Would the minister be kind enough to explain what influenced him in deciding that new potatoes must be graded? It would appear to be rather a new departure. New potatoes are, as the word implies, essentially immature and of small size. Consequently they command a higher price on account of people being willing to pay for a new article, so to speak. If these new potatoes are to come under the inspection provisions, they will have to be of a certain size and reasonably mature. Why was it deemed necessary to bring them under this measure?

We have received a number of requests from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick that all potatoes there be graded; that, as a matter of fact, grading be made compulsory and the potatoes covered by a certificate of inspection. In addition to that we have these resolutions: resolution by the Canadian Horticultural Council asking that new potatoes be .brought under the same regulations as other potatoes; resolution by the Ontario Vegetable Growers' Association; also resolutions by the South Essex Growers' Cooperative and the Central Ontario Potato Growers' Association.

I think this is another way of getting at something which the government
Root Vegetables Act

attempted to do some time ago. It will be recalled that the government passed an order in council fixing a price, for duty purposes, on potatoes. There was a great deal of protest against that order in council, and the government, instead of rescinding it when the evils of it were pointed out, passed another order in council. Like the laws of the Medes and Persians, I suppose their orders are unchangeable. So they passed another order in council substituting radishes for potatoes. The effect of the first order in council was to put a heavy impost on new potatoes coming into this country. Objections were raised by American shippers, and these objections were endorsed by the potato growers of the maritime provinces, who were accustomed to sell large quantities of seed potatoes to the United States, which trade was going to be endangered. By bringing down this amendment the government is seeking to do in another way what they were prevented from doing in the first place. Now they are going to apply grading regulations in such a way that the small potatoes that come in in the early spring will be excluded because they will not come up to the grading regulations. As a matter of fact, that is the purpose of this bill. Instead of calling it a bill to amend the Root Vegetables Act, we might as well call it an act to exclude new potatoes coming in from the United States.
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that is why the Horticultural Council and these other associations have requested this legislation?
Yes, absolutely, and nothing else.

I understand from the minister that a number of bodies have asked for this legislation. I am not particularly opposing the legislation in that regard, but I should like some further information. Under chapter 181 of the revised statutes, the various grades of potato are defined, such as Canada A, Canada B, Canada C, and so on, and I think in all cases the potatoes are required to be reasonably mature, and even the lowest grade, grade C, is required to be I think not less than li inches in diameter. Subsequently it appears-I have not the act before me-that the ex-Minister of Agriculture, in 1929 I think it was, changed that definition section of the act and did away with direct definitions of the various grades. Instead he made regulations which allowed his department, with the advice of certain bodies therein indicated, to make new definitions each year of what constituted the different grades, based apparently

upon what has 'been done in the matter of grading wheat every year. I do not think that idea was a sound one because potatoes are of a more stable character than wheat, and the same grade or the same size should apply every year, one would suppose. Nevertheless that is what was done. In the event of the grades not being defined in any act, I presume that we shall have to fall back on the order in council or the definition which the minister or his department will give every year. What I am trying to get at is this: Under the present definition-it may be changed in a few weeks or a few months-what will be the smallest size of potato that will be allowed in now that they have to be graded?

If this section passes. I take it that the new potatoes will be subject to the grades as set out now for the old potatoes, but if there is sufficient evidence that the potato growers wish to have new grades or the exemption of certain grades of new potatoes, that can be put into effect by a ministerial order at their request.

With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alfoerni (Mr. Neill), there is a very great necessity at times of the department having the power to change the grades. You can see how necessary it was to change those regulations, because a carload of potatoes consisting wholly of potatoes from 1J to 2J inches is of very inferior calibre, and nobody would accept it. They gave me to understand they would put a seasonal duty on American potatoes to encourage the Canadian grower along the St. John river and in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. I am sure potato growers in the central provinces will tell you that they do not want this inferior stuff to come in when they are trying to clear off their old stock in Toronto, Montreal and our other Canadian markets. Surely the committee must misunderstand the situation or there would not be a single voice raised against this bill. There ought not to be a single protest against the passing of this measure, which has been asked for by our potato growers for a number of years past. I think the ex-Minister of Agriculture will remember that when I saw him three years ago I told him the farmers in New Brunswick were getting 10 cents a bushel for their potatoes. The farmers of Ontario. Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island would like to sell the balance of their old stock before their new stock comes on the market. I know the ex-Minister of Agriculture was sympathetic towards my proposal, and I do not know why a seasonal duty was not imposed at that time. We went home on that occasion and had to dump thousands of bushels of our potatoes into the river or take them out into the fields and let them rot.

Was any request received
from the province of Quebec?
From the cooperative associations. In reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I did not try to evade answering his question.
Oh, no.

I thought he would
have the information. If it is the wish of the committee 1 will give the different grades. One and a half inches in diameter-that is the Canadian number 3.
And reasonably matured?
No, that applies to 1 and 2.

This is Canada
number 3:

I do not intend to continue my opposition to this bill. I spoke as I did in order to call attention to the real nature of the bill which was being introduced under one name when the intention was in a measure hidden. I thought it well also to call the attention of the house and the country to the exact position in which we on both sides of the house stand to-day in regard to some of these matters. I called attention to it also in order to furnish another illustration of the kind of policy the government are pursuing. If it is our intention absolutely to exclude American goods-and there can be no question that is the intention of this bill- in order that the old stock may be cleaned up, do not let us beat about the bush. We tried one method, by passing certain orders in council, and found that it did not work; there were many protests against it. Now we are trying this other method, and probably there will be protests against it as well. If we want to exclude foreign goods, let us put an embargo against them and be done with it.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see anything very alarming about this bill. Some of us are so sensitive on tariff matters that we can see them in every woodpile. This bill is simply an evolution of the grading system, as I understand it, as applied to potatoes. If I were to oppose the bill I would be opposing the policy we have followed as a government for the last seven or eight years.
Formerly these new potatoes were exempt from grading, the reason being that we thought we were applying the principle of grading just about as fast as the people would accept it. Many a raking over I received in this house, when I was on the other side, for shoving the grading policy of the government ahead with regard to all kinds of farm products including vegetables. We did not think we crowded it, but we kept well up to public sentiment in the matter. We thought public sentiment was not sufficiently crystallized to approve of the grading of new potatoes at that time, but perhaps public sentiment has developed since then and it has been found that the departmental regulations we were authorized to make under the

Root Vegetables Act

amending act of 1929 should be extended to cover new potatoes. The departmental officials and the growers, after sizing up the situation and getting suggestions from their organizations, have been setting the grades during the last two years for vegetables such as carrots, turnips, parsnips and so on, and they have been working out splendidly. There has not been a single complaint, so far as I know, with regard to the grades which have been worked out between the departmental officials and the organizations of growers throughout the country. The intention here is to apply the same style of grading and the same principle of cooperation between departmental officials and organizations of growers to new potatoes, which formerly were exempt from grading.
I think that is right. We cannot very well say exactly, as my hon. friend from Victoria-Carleton indicated, what the grades will be until the regulations have been agreed upon. I presume the departmental officials and the growers already have in mind the regulations which will be adopted as soon as this bill is put through. That is my anticipation, so I would not think the minister could say now exactly what they will be. They may be approximately the same as they were before; they will be the same until the growers and the departmental officials get together and evolve such regulations and grades as are applicable to conditions which exist to-day. That will not be done until this act passes, as I understand it. After that is done, then new potatoes will be graded exactly as other vegetables have been graded for the last two years.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Agriculture if these grades will apply to potatoes which the farmer may bring to the market in open containers.
That is one question which will be decided between the producers ond the departmental officials, as the former Minister of Agriculture has said.

There are too many things up in the air, as far as this bill is concerned; there are too many things which are to be settled at some future date. I think we have had too much of that legislation already.

I think
it is only fair to enlighten the hon. member a little on that point.

You do not know; how
can you enlighten me when the minister cannot?	-
I presume the minister could enlighten you more than I can, but I suppose I have the same privilege the hon. member has.

Are you speaking for the
government?

I am
not speaking for the government; I am trying to enlighten the hon. member for Lisgar. The first potatoes which are dug out of the field are not quite mature enough to be placed in bags or packages, and under the old regulations of the Department of Agriculture farmers were allowed to ship those potatoes in bulk for a certain time. After that we were compelled to put them in bags, or at least during a portion of last year we were compelled to do so. There is a very strong movement on foot to-day, which was voiced very strongly at the meeting last summer of the Eastern Canada Fruit and Vegetable Growers' Association, held in St. John, that all potatoes should be shipped in packages. I am not so sure that this should be done as far as it applies to the very early shipments, and I think the matter is left in that way so that the very early shipments we make might be shipped in bulk rather than in packages or bags or barrels.

I just want
to say a few words in regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), who seems so partial to United States potatoes and so much opposed to Canadian potatoes. I made a remark a little while ago about the class of potatoes being sold in Canada coming from the United States, and called them trash. I should like to exhibit one potato. It is less than an inch in size and full of disease of all kinds. It has powdery scab and other diseases. I picked it out of a barrel exhibited for sale on Bank street a few days ago, coming from the United States. Is this committee satisfied?
Is that an average?

No, I will
say it is not an average, but it was exhibited for sale. There were a number of others equally bad, and there was some better stuff in the barrel as well.
Do you think anybody would buy it?

A few
moments ago the hon. member for Weyburn said the people had discretion enough to buy or not buy as they saw fit. That stuff is coming into Canada and is being placed on

Root Vegetables Act
the market for sale, and I presume that would not be done unless there were buyers. My point is that stuff like this should be shut out.

I should like to direct attention to a point which I think is of some importance in connection with our procedure. When the house went into committee on this bill the deputy speaker, who was then in the chair, insisted very strongly that section 1 had been carried. Some of us protested that it had not been carried at the previous sitting, and there was good reason why that was not done; the Minister of Agriculture was not in his place at the time. All that is recorded in the votes and proceedings is this:
The bill No. 87, an act to amend the Root Vegetable Act. was considered in committee of the whole, and progress having been made and reported, the committee obtained leave to consider it again at the next sitting of the house.
That is a contradiction of the statement of the deputy speaker that section 1 was carried at the last sitting.

There is no doubt that was
the case; further than that, section 1 is not in correct form. It should read:
Section 6 of the Root Vegetables Act, chapter 181, revised statutes of Canada, as amended by act of 1929-
I do not think it is good law as it reads now. We are repealing a section which already has been repealed by a subsequent enactment, so this section should begin with the words I have indicated.
I am not opposing this particular matter; possibly there is some merit in the suggestion, but I think we are overdoing the whole thing as a governing body. We are overdoing this principle of grading in these hard times; we are interfering with business by grading this and grading the other thing. I anticipate that the day will come, Mr. Chairman, when we will be grading babies; those under a certain size and length will be excluded, I presume.

In regard to the suggestion
last made, as to the form of the bill, I looked into this matter after the last sitting, at the request of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, and I think there is no doubt but that this amending act is drafted in proper form. It is an amendment to chapter 181 of the revised statutes, and section 6 is repealed. Section 6 in the revised statutes, which is now repealed, was not changed by the amending act of 1929; but with regard to section 19, one clause was amended though it remained as a part of section 19 of the Root Vegetables Act, chapter 181 of the revised 22110-1891
statutes of Canada. The whole section is now repealed and certainly the bill is in proper form.

It is always the custom to
say "as amended by" and then to cite the later act. That is all I know about it.

There may be differences
in different acts, but I am sure this is drafted in proper form to carry out the intention. I looked into it very carefully after the last debate.

Mr. Chairman,
since we are being permitted to discuss section 1 might I ask the Secretary of State if he does not think this is rather confusing. It refers to an act which has nothing whatever to do with the amended section. All that is necessary is to say "as amended by" and then state the act of 1929. That would solve the problem so that we laymen would not be worrying about something which is not here.

For the information of those who may study the bill it is marked on the margin, "revised statutes, chapter 181; acts of 1929, chapter 7." This is an amendment to chapter 181 of the revised statutes, and one section is repealed that was not amended in 1929. Another section, No. 19, is repealed in its entirety, so there need be no confusion about it.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid there is some confusion, but it is on the other side of the house. If you look up the chapter mentioned you will find it does not refer to this business of potatoes at all. If you look up the amended act of 1929, you will find that section 3, subsection
(d)	states:
. Prescribing brands or marks and the manner m which same shall be placed on vegetable containers.
All we have to do in order to avoid confusion is to say "as amended by chapter 7 of the acts of 1929." Why not mention that in the bill, and not have us hunting all over creation for it?

It may be necessary for the information of the hon. gentleman, but if he will look in the index to any one of the annual statutes he always will be able to see what amendments to the revised statutes have been made. If I am looking at a revised statute I always look at the index to see what amendments have been made since those statutes were brought into force, but I am speaking now of the legal effect of the draft-
Root Vegetables Act

ing of this bill. It is in proper form, and it effects the object which the Minister of Agriculture has in view. That is all.

That may be so, but I have had some experience with the way the law officers here maul bills sent from the Department of Agriculture. As I understand it, this bill originally contained the words "as amended in 1929" but it went through the hands of the law officers here, and they have their own notions as to draftsmanship. Very often they fix bills up so delightfully that they mean something altogether different from what was meant by the department in the first place. I have had to withdraw bills from the order paper after they had gone through the hands of the law officers, so if the minister wants to keep out of the trouble caused by the law officers of the crown mutilating his bills, of course with the best intentions in the world, I suggest that, before they go on the order paper, he or his officers look them over and see if they can recognize them as the same bills which were sent from the department. If they are not the same, or if they do not mean the same thing, they should be corrected before going on the order paper. I had to do that for seven yeans, after having been caught badly. The former leader of the Conservative party, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, certainly went after me for having brought down a bill which had to be withdrawn because it was improperly drafted by the law officers. It meant something entirely different from what was intended by the department. I had to withdraw it and go through that humiliation, and I should like to save the minister the experience I had. It is the only way he can save himself; it is up to him to see that the bill is in the form lie desires it to be, and not as the law officers think it should be.

I would not for a moment argue with the Secretary of State as to the legality of this bill; that would be very presumptuous on my part, but I do appeal to him from the standpoint of a man who wants to look up the law. We know the statutes are only revised once in ten years. Nine years from now this is what may happen: I may look up this act and find that it reads as it is here; in regard to the section which is being struck out it says:
The section quoted above provides specifically for the marking of packages which contain potatoes and onions. Provisions for this are already made under section 3 (d) of the act.
So I will turn to this act and look for section 3 (d), but there is no section 3 (d) in it.
(Mr. Cahan.]
If it only said "as amended by the act of 1929'' then I could readily turn up the act of 1929 and put my finger on the amendment. Nine years after it has been amended, however, I may have to reason like this: "There is no section 3 (d) in the original act; therefore it must have been amended by one of the acts passed during the following nine years." Then I will have to look up the acts of each of those nine years, and, as any lawyer would have to do the same, to see when that amendment was made. Would it not be worth while to put in a few extra words in older to make it a little more easily ascertainable, even to legal men?
I should like a little information from the minister. Is the description of the grades of these new' potatoes fixed by statute or by regulation?
By regulation.
The minister w'as reading something to the house; was that from the regulations?

Yes, vegetable
grades and regulations.
When were they made?
June 29 and August 3, 1929.

Could the minister tell me under what section of the act these regulations were made? I have consulted the act, perhaps in its original form, and I gather that section 3 fixes the dimensions of the grades absolutely. Has that been changed?

I was reading from vegetable grades and regulations, published in the Canada Gazette of June 29 and August 3, 1929, under and by virtue of the powers conferred upon the minister by subsection 1; section 3 of the Root Vegetables Act, chapter 181 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, as amended by chapter 7 of the statutes of 1929.

If the size which the minister mentions is found to be too large, can it be changed by the department from time to time? Would the minister mind telling the size again? I should have listened more attentively, I suppose.
Does the hon. gentleman mean the entire description, or the minimum size?
The minimum size.

The minimum diameter of the lowest grades shall not be less than 1J inches.

Root Vegetables Act
29S1
If that remains without change, will it keep any considerable quantity of potatoes off the market?
I would say, yes.

I want the minister to understand that I am asking for information only. I am under the impression that the validity of these grading acts is questionable, although I may be entirely mistaken as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is concurrent legislation.
The Minister of Justice says that there is concurrent legislation; is there to be concurrent legislation, or is there concurrent legislation already?

speechtext: There is already.
In all provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand so.

If that is so, all right, but
if not then there should be such legislation.
So far as the grading regulations are concerned they cannot be fixed by statute. It is necessary that they be changed from time to time as occasion warrants.
That was the case up until a year or two ago.

Then the change was made, and rightly so. In the ease of the crop of 1929 the minimum size for No. 1 certified seed was 2J- inches, but it was found that there was a scarcity of potatoes in the United States. There was a greater demand for this No. 1 certified seed than could be supplied, so'much so that the buyers from the southern states were willing to accept the smaller grade, down to two inches and even as low as 1J inches. Several steamer loads of potatoes with a minimum size of 1| inches were exported that year, although these potatoes were grown from certified stock in inspected fields. Before our inspectors could give a certificate covering these potatoes smaller than 2J inches they had to receive the sanction of the Department of Agriculture. We could not have waited until parliament was in session in order to have this change made.
(Huron): What regulation or order in council was passed on April 22, 1931, with respect to potatoes?

I could not answer
that question offhand.

My information is that that order in council was rescinded
eight days afterward and in the interval the farmers of southwestern Ontario had planted thousands of acres of potatoes with the expectation of having a market therefor. My information is that this present change is for the purpose of getting the government out of a difficulty.
Is the hon. member speaking of the dumping duty?
(Huron): For the year ended December 31, 1930, we exported to the United States five times as many potatoes as we imported.
What has that got to do with this bill?

I have no doubt that this is being done at the instance of the secretary of the Horticultural Council, who has been going around the country to find out what can be done in order to save the potato growers of western Ontario from the importation of early potatoes from the United States.
I think the whole thing is a farce and it should be left alone.
Has my point of order been sustained?
Clause 1 is passed, but it will not be recorded in the votes and proceedings until the bill is passed.

I do not know whether or not I understood correctly the hon. member for Vietoria-Carleton (Mr. Smith) when he referred to a number of cars of small potatoes accumulating on the other side of the line and which were dumped in here almost free.

They
charged only a low price.

The hon. member did not mean free of duty, but at a low price, which is a different matter. What should be guarded against is doing anything to injure the potato industry of the maritime provinces. As I understand this amendment, potatoes grown in the vicinity of the different cities throughout the dominion can be marketed in open containers and will not be subject to grading. Am I correct in that?
Yes.

Potatoes coming in from the United States come in in closed containers, and the object of this amendment is to shut out importations from the United States. Recently an order in council was passed fixing a value of six cents per pound for duly purposes, but this resulted in a great deal of
29S2
Root Vegetables Act

confusion and misunderstanding throughout the Dominion. The United States shippers of potatoes to Canada went up in the air about it and they got after our friends in Canada and the result was that this government rescinded that order in council and, as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) has said, substituted the word "radishes" for the word "potatoes." When the Liberal party was in power it was charged that it was under domination from Washington, that it was following out a made-in-Washington policy, but if there ever was domination from Washington, this particular case is an illustration. When that restriction on American potatoes was put on they got after the minister and endeavoured to have it corrected, with the result that it was taken off and American potatoes up until the present time have been allowed to come in at the old rate. Speaking as a Prince Edward Islander, I desire to say that the one thing we should guard against at the present time is the jeopardizing of this industry. If this present proposal is similar, in effect) to the one which put a six cents per pound valuation for duty purposes on potatoes, then I think we should be careful in passing it; if this regulation is for the benefit of the industry, then we should support it.
Does the hon. member know what it is?

What did the hon. member
say?
I was just wondering if the hon. member knows what it is.

I am asking only for information; I want to know what the effect of this legislation will be. My hon. friend is a very esteemed lawyer down in our part of the country and there is no doubt he can give a correct interpretation of this bill, but I find it difficult to discover the exact meaning. The shippers in this vicinity will not be affected because the potatoes will not have to be graded, but potatoes coming in from the United States are subject to grade and my contention is that this bill will exclude those potatoes and possibly have the same effect as had the other regulation. I think it is up to the hon. members from the maritime provinces to express their views on this matter. We should be sure that we are doing something for the benefit of the industry, rather than to injure it.

I think there is a great deal in what the hon. gentleman has just said. Although it may not be a ground for opposition to this section, it certainly is a ground for a suggestion to the minister and to the

government that they be very careful in framing the regulations. It is quite true that when a high valuation for duty purposes was placed by the government upon potatoes protests were received from our customers in the United States. The exporters to the United States became alarmed and went to the government and prevailed upon them to do away with the high valuation for duty purposes. If this bill does what the Minister of Agriculture says it will do, shut off the market for a considerable quantity of American potatoes, you will have similar protests, and if the government acts upon the same principle as it did before, I anticipate it will change the regulations so as to let in smaller potatoes. Whether it is desirable to have this excessive instability in such matters, is questionable. I do not think anything has caused more unfavourable criticism in the maritime provinces than the great instability of the government's tariff policy, their habit of one day fixing valuations which they take off the next day, their habit of imposing dumping duties and tariffs which are later removed. My suggestion to the minister is that possibly under this legislation or under the regulations made under it we shall have that unsatisfactory condition of instability continued; we shall have rapid changes and fluctuations in the regulations with regard to the size of these new potatoes. If the size is made too large, a considerable quantity of importations will be shut off. This will cause protests from our foreign customers and delegations from friends of the government asking the government to change the regulations. I should like to have the minister's view whether that is not a very real danger in what is contemplated under this legislation.

The information
given me is that the strongest requests for grading to include all potatoes have come from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, from the maritimes. To show the thoroughness with which grading has been done. I am informed that out of 6.623 cars inspected last year in Prince Edward Island, the grading was reversed in only one case and that out of 8,455 cars from New Brunswick, 99 were objected to, but the decision of the graders was reversed in only 14 cases. It is only fair to say that the people from the maritimes who sell their seed potatoes at the good prices at which they do sell them, realize that this is on account of the thorough inspection that is made there, which keeps the potatoes free from disease and maintains a very high quality. I took every reasonable care in the matter. The bill was under con-

Supply-Pensions
sideration long before any order in council was passed, and so far as I am concerned was quite free from any connection with it.
I made every inquiry that I could as to how this would be received by the farmers, by the potato growers, and the information given to me is to the effect that little if any objection to grading is raised now by the farmers. Some time ago, as the former Minister of Agriculture said, until the people were educated to grading and realized the benefit of it, there was a good deal of objection, but I believe that has entirely passed away. At one meeting which the commissioner held in Prince Edward Island and which was attended by approximately 700 people, no one voiced any complaint as regards grading.

I do not want to be understood as objecting to grading from the point of view of improving the quality of the farm product. I believe the quality of farm products can be and has been improved by the system of grading, but I object to the use of this system to accomplish a purpose for which it was not intended, a purpose entirely apart from the question of improving the quality of farm products.

Can the minister give the
information supplied to- him by those who asked for this legislation?

The information is
much the same in each communication from both individuals and associations, namely, that they wished the grading to include all potatoes.
Did they say why?

Were any representations
made from British Columbia to maintain the duty in view of the fact that potatoes had entered British Columbia from China while thousands of tons were stored in British Columbia?
We are not discussing tariffs.

This is merely a matter
of extending to new potatoes the system of grading as already applied to old potatoes. This will not prevent any man in the United States from shipping to Canada No. 2 or No. 3 potatoes, but it will make him grade and classify his potatoes and make him ship No. 3 as No. 3, No. 2 as No. 2 and No. 1 as No. 1. He will not be able to jumble them all together and put them on the market in Canada as No. 1. I do not think we are imposing anything against the United States that we are not imposing on ourselves.
The government is just putting new potatoes on a parity with other potatoes.
That is all.

This has nothing
to do with duties or valuations.

The only difference I see is that local potatoes will come in bulk ungraded, whereas potatoes entering in closed containers will certainly have to be graded, so that if the people of the United States look at it in that light, they will feel there is quite a preference in favour of local shippers. As regards the minister's remarks in connection with grading, I quite agree with him that the farmers and the people generally of Prince Edward Island arc 100 per cent for grading. In fact, we were, I think, one of the first provinces to ask for compulsory grading of potatoes, and not a carload is shipped out of that province ungraded. The benefits to the growers have been great. I am not opposing the bill at all if it is going to be of benefit to the industry, but if there is any possibility of its resulting in injury we should proceed carefully and look into every phase of the legislation before it is adopted.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Professor Shortt had rendered very great public service, and this was the position to which, I think, all parties were agreeable that he should be appointed.

I think that statement is pretty much what was to be expected from the minister. The minister is aware that there are branches of the archives in Montreal,

Supply-Secretary oj State
also in the maritime provinces. While I was in charge of the department there was a demand to establish a branch in the western provinces. I admit that this would necessitate the voting of additional moneys, but perhaps the minister would state whether the matter is still under consideration.

Representations have been made, and I met a delegation from the west, but at present it seems inopportune to make any definite decision about the matter, and it remains as it was when my hon. friend left office.
Of course, this matter should come up under vote 345.

I notice that recently there has been published, apparently by the authority of the Secretary of State, under the direction of the keeper of the records, a book entitled: A Collection of Documents Relating to Jacques Cartier and the Sieur de Roberval by H. P. Biggar, D. Litt., chief archivist for Canada in Europe. I have not seen the book, but from a notice that appears in Le Devoir, it seems that it contains an English translation of certain Spanish documents, but no French translation. Both the introduction and the table of contents are also in the English language. I am sure the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) desires to have the two languages recognized in all our official publications, particularly in those of his department.

I am entirely in sympathy with my hon. friend's position, but I may say that the work to which he refers was commenced a considerable time ago under the regime of my hon. friend the late Secretary of State. I know the book was carried almost to completion in October, when I first saw a printed proof in London. The greater part of the book, if I remember correctly, contains copies of the original French and Spanish documents, but a translation of the latter into English is included. I presume that those who had charge of the work felt that this course might serve the purposes of historical research, because Spanish is so easy to those who read French. The book was issued a short time after I assumed office, but I have had no responsibility beyond that.
I think there should be an edition in French as well as in English.

If I remember correctly, my hon. predecessor arranged for the printing of this book in England, because of the facilities there for printing in Spanish, and there the proof had to be read and compared with the
original Spanish documents. It is a most interesting book and I recommend it to those members who take an interest in the archives of Canada. If my hon. friend thinks it necessary that another edition should be put out-
I think there should be a French edition.
I will consider the matter with the officials of the department.
Seeing that both languages are official, I would ask the government to give instructions as soon as possible to have a French edition issued.

My recollection is that this is not exactly a publication of the department, but a book published by Mr. Biggar. On account of its special interest, the department contributed a certain sum to ensure publication, very much in the same way as we subscribe for a certain number of copies to help an author publish his book, but by so doing we take no responsibility for the publication. I endorse the stand taken by the hon. member (Mr. Casgrain), but it being Mr. Biggar's book, I think the committee will understand the responsibility of the archives department stops where Mr. Biggar's begins.

I made this request because the book apparently is published by the authority of the Secretary of State under the direction of the keeper of the records. Therefore it would appear to be an official publication.

I will see what arrangements can be made to meet the views of my hon. friend. I have done nothing with regard to the publication, the arrangements for which were made under the regime of my hon. friend still continue.

May I make this general statement in regard to the archives department? When I was in charge, it was represented to me very often by Doctor Doughty- who everybody knows is a very capable deputy -that the department has not enough money at its disposal. When the department has disposed of the money voted for these purposes, that is, keeping up the branches I have referred to, and certain special work which is done during the summer, there is very little money left with which the department can acquire documents, books and things of that kind. It is true that they may ask for a special credit or estimate for that purpose, but it has been my experience and probably will be the experience of my successor that this is not easily available.
Supply-Secretary of State

I think it would be worth while considering, perhaps not this year because of the economies being practised in many directions, but in coming years, if the amount placed at the disposal of the dominion archivist should not be increased very materially. Every month there are libraries, books, paintings or documents offered on the public market, for which this government cannot compete through lack of funds. Only recently it was brought to my attention that Mr. Victor Morin of Montreal had disposed of many valuable books having to do with the history of Canada, some of them unique in their contents and general importance and interest. I do not think the archives branch was able to compete for any of them. Most of those books were sold to the United States.
Again I say this is not a criticism. I know the conditions and I am merely making a statement, which perhaps I should have made when I was minister, in all good faith. I hope that in future estimates, when the prosperity predicted by the Prime Minister has come back, it will be possible for my hon. friend to ask for an increased amount for the archives branch, which will enable the archivist to compete in the purchase of such documents and books as I have mentioned. I do not think $25,000 would be too much, and I can assure my hon. friend that if he asks for such an increase in an}1 coming year he will have my very frank support.

(Mr. Rinfret.]

When I came into office in
August last I found that a number of representations had been made with regard to the fraudulent issue of certificates of naturalization. A further inquiry was made by the officers of the department, who subsequently asked for the assistance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Judge Wallace of the county court of Woodstock, Ontario, was appointed a commissioner to conduct this investigation. Some expense was incurred, and more will be incurred in connection with that investigation, which is not yet complete.
The additional reason is that under the old age pensions act, only those who are naturalized British subjects can receive pensions, and in whichever province the pensions act is brought into force a large number of applications are made for naturalization, many of them by very old settlers, in order that they may come under the terms of that act. The result is that there has been and is likely to be during this ensuing year a further additional expense under the Naturalization Act, and therefore we have increased the appropriation. The habit has been, as I think my hon. friend will bear witness, rather to exceed the appropriation in recent years. This has left a debit balance, which naturally has had to be carried over to the ensuing fiscal year. This increase is to straighten out the accounts and to provide for some slight increase in the cost of administering that act during the ensuing year.
I understand Judge Wallace has found irregularities in connection with some 150 cases.
Some 170, I think.

Will the
minister tell us what has been done in connection with those cases? Have any deportations been effected as a result of the findings?

There is but one penalty
under the act. In each one of these cases the naturalization has been revoked. Judge Wallace is preparing a report which I hope to submit to the Department of Justice, to obtain advice as to whether in certain cases criminal prosecution should be proceeded with. But we have not yet reached that stage. From a personal conversation with Judge Wallace I inferred that he thought in many instances that those who had received naturalization certificates fraudulently had been imposed upon by others who wished to obtain fees for procuring the certificates. In several instances he thought the applicants

Supply-Secretary oj State
had been perfectly innocent. Foreigners coming in and residing here had been imposed upon, thinking that they were applying for naturalization certificates in the regular way. As to whether those who deceived them should be prosecuted or not, that is a matter for the Department of Justice to decide.

Has Judge Wallace been
appointed to deal only with fraudulent cases, or has he been appointed to act in some other capacity as well? Earlier in the session I placed on the order paper certain questions with respect to naturalization, and Hansard showed that there appeared to be some confusion. I thought I would wait until this occasion to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. The minister is aware that his department will recommend the revocation of certificates of naturalization for certain deficiencies in respect to the residence qualification. That is done by order in council. Such certificates are revoked not because they have been fraudulently obtained but because the subject has not resided in this country, or for some other reason. Those certificates are revoked by order in council. But I understand that the subject has the right to appeal, and if he does appeal, the case should go before a commissioner. Now, such a commissioner does not exist. The question I put to the Secretary of State earlier in the session was whether he had appointed a commissioner to deal with these ases, and his reply was that Judge Wallace had been appointed. I understand, however, that Judge Wallace is dealing only with fraudulent cases in a special inquiry.

There are two classes of
cases. There is one class, a very limited one, in respect of which the Secretary of State may rescind certificates previously granted. But in respect of these 170 cases which have been reported adversely upon-I am speaking from memory; the number may be more or less-they could be acted upon under the statute only after an inquiry had been conducted by one having judicial experience. Upon the report of such a commissioner hay-mg judicial experience, the matter is brought, and in each case has been brought, to the attention of the governor in council, and orders in council have been passed carrying into effect the findings of the judge sitting as *ommissioner.

I thank the minister for
his reply. When Judge Wallace is through dealing with these fraudulent Cases, will he be retained as commissioner on naturalization
cases?

No. I do not know what
section of the act my hon. friend has in mind.
If my hon. friend will let me have the act I will point out to him later on what I mean.

I may be mistaken, but I
do not think there is any appeal from the findings of this commissioner. He makes a finding, and the matter is then brought to the governor in council, and the governor in council by order in council revokes the naturalization certificate previously granted. And that procedure has been followed quite closely. Section 9 of the Naturalization Act, subsection 4, provides:
An inquiry under this section shall be held by a commission constituted for the purpose by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the minister, presided over by a person appointed by the governor in council, who holds or has held high judicial office, and shall be conducted in such manner as the governor in council shall direct, provided that any such inquiry may, if the governor in council thinks fit, instead of being held as aforesaid, be held by the superior court of the province in which the case arises, and the practice and procedure on any inquiry so held shall be regulated hy rules of court.
As evidence in these cases had to be taken in Ottawa as well as Montreal and Toronto, it was deemed best to appoint a special commissioner having judicial qualifications for the purpose. And that is the procedure that has been followed.

It is no doubt desirable to prevent people from obtaining naturalization certificates by fraudulent means. But I should like to inquire with regard to the possibility of some people being prevented from obtaining naturalization who really ought to have it. As I understand it, the recommendation for naturalization is made by the judge, whose decision the Secretary of State follows. It seems to me there ought to be some appeal against the decision of some of our judges in order that people who are desirable should be assured of receiving naturalization. I have in mind two classes. First of all, there are some elderly people who have been living in remote districts and who have not been able to acquire a good knowledge of English. I think particularly of one old woman who is now almost destitute. She has never had an opportunity of learning English, having resided in a very remote district. She ought to come under the Old Age Pensions Act, but she is not eligible because she has not a knowledge of the language. Possibly the judge is only carrying out his duty when he insists that she

Supply-Secretary of State

should have a good knowledge of English or French. But it seems to me that the act ought to be somewhat liberally interpreted, and if a local judge is very rigid in his interpretation of it there should be an appeal, so that such a person might obtain naturalization and so come under the Old Age Pensions Act.
Then there is a second class, in connection with which a great many cases have been referred to me. I refer to labouring men of foreign extraction who have been adversely reported upon by some of the police. They may have been reported upon years ago, and this stands against them. We hope to make them good citizens, but in the meantime they are absolutely disfranchised. There is no opportunity for them to participate in the citizenship of the country. In certain instances I am sure that the adverse report of the judge has been based upon local prejudices, and in these cases there ought to be an appeal. If necessary, some other judge should hear the case. While we ought to stand guard over our citizenship, we ought, on the other hand, to welcome to that citizenship everyone who is likely to become a good citizen. I do not know just what provision should be made but I desire to call the attention of the Secretary of State to the matter. Possibly he may know of some way in which this matter can be adjusted.

A ruling was made during
the time of the Hon. Mr. Doherty, and I think was thereafter adhered to by the Department of Justice during the last regime, under which an instruction was given to the judges that as long as an applicant could make himself or herself understood in either the French or the English language it was not necessary in order to comply with the law, that he or she could speak and write the English or French language. That widened the scope of the inquiry before the judge in favour of many applicants, especially in the provinces of the northwest. Nevertheless, as to character and general qualification for citizenship the judge presiding at the court of the district must, under the act as at present construed, give the final decision as to qualification. Since I have been in office I have not overruled the decision of any judge in such a case and I think that that was the experience of my hon. predecessor in office.

I can give a very
good illustration of that regulation with regard to the knowledge of English. This case was brought to my attention several years ago by one of the charity organizations in a western city. The judge asked some question,

I think it was as to who the governor general was, and the applicant for naturalization did not know the answer. The judge took th : stand that if a matter which seemed to him to be so simple was not known to the applicant that he was not eligible for citizenship. That to me is perfectly absurd, and it seems to me that when a judge takes that stand there should be some appeal. It is not fair to those who are in every other way qualified for citizenship to be barred because they have not had any wide reading.

During a former session my
hon. friend the member for St. James (Mr Rinfret), then Secretary of State, introduced a bill giving to the office of the Secretary of State a very much wider scope and discretion in the matter of naturalization. I opposed it at the time upon the ground that it might open the way to political intrigue and that sort of thing. As I have gone into this matter and studied the material which was before my hon. friend when he introduced that bill, I have come to the conclusion that there were much stronger grounds in its favour than I had anticipated.
Why did the hon. member oppose it?
There would be no question of political intrigue now?

I am simply saying quite
frankly that when one sits in the house and hears merely the discussion on a particular bill he may place a certain interpretation upon it, but when he has had experience in the administration of an office-
Hear, hear.

When one is in possession of full information as to the documents on file and has knowledge of the representations which have been made and discussions which have ensued, a certain effect is made upon one's judgment.

I am delighted to hear
the Secretary of State make the statement which he has. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will remember that in a former session, I think it was 1928, the house sat for five or six days discussing a bill tn do away with the requirement that an applicant for naturalization should have to go before a judge. That bill passed this house but unfortunately was repealed by the Senate. I do not think it is desirable to reopen that discussion, although I am not trying to preclude my hon. friend from doing so. I should like to go back to the point I raised a moment

Supply-Secretary of State
ago. I have the statute before me, and I would refer the committee to section 9 of the Naturalization Act. That section deals with ihe revocation of certificates of naturalization by governor in council on report of the Secretary of State, and subsection 2 covers the oases wherein the certificates may be revoked, as follows:
(a)	trading with an enemy,
(b)	serving a term of imprisonment,
(c)	bad character,
fd) non-residence for seven years,
(e)	an enemy subject.
My experience has been that the Secretary of State recommends to the governor in council the revocation'of a certain number of certificates under the non-residence clause, but I would refer my hon. friend to subsection 3, which reads:
The minister may if he thinks fit before making a report under this section refer the case for such inquiry as is hereinafter specified, and in any case to which subsection one, or paragraphs (a), (c) or (e) of subsection two of this section applies, the minister shall by notice given to or sent to the last known address of the holder of the certificate give him an opportunity of claiming that the case be referred for such inquiry, and if the holder so claims in accordance with the notice, the minister shall refer the case for inquiry accordingly.
That is what I had in mind when I spoke of appeal. That may not have been the proper word to use, but I think the meaning is there. In certain cases, before the minister can revoke a certificate, he must give notice to the candidate and if the candidate desires an inquiry he must hold one. Subsection 4 reads as follows:
An inquiry under this section shall be held by a commission constituted for the purpose by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the minister, presided over by a person appointed by the governor in council who holds or has held high judicial office.
While I was at the head of the department there was some difficulty in finding a commissioner who could qualify under subsection 4, because it was not passible to offer any remuneration to a judge in office, and it was hard to find a man having judicial qualifications who could act under this section and who would perhaps have to travel from one end of the country to the other. I asked the minister a moment ago if Judge Wallace had been appointed merely to deal with fraudulent cases in a special inquiry or whether he was to act as a commissioner to pass on cases such as are mentioned in this section of the act.

Judge Wallace was appointed to consider any case which I might refer to
him under the act. His appointment is during pleasure and is not permanent. It is not anticipated that for a year or more I will refer to him all cases which may arise. He is a judge of the county court, possessing wide experience and holding a high reputation, and was willing to accept this task. I hope to have included in the supplementary estimates a small solatium to Judge Wallace because he has performed excellent work at very great expense to himself.
That would mean if Mr. Justice Wallace carries on for three years more, perhaps we on this side will appoint his successor.
I should think Judge Wallace would not carry on beyond the year. There is no intention to make this a permanent or semi-permanent employment.

Is there any possibility of putting the material of the Canada Gazette in a more convenient form? It is almost impossible for the ordinary man to find out what is in it. Apparently a number of old forms are followed. I had occasion once bo try to find out when parliament would meet, and apparently the date was put over from week to week; I do not know just the underlying reason but I got quite excited when I saw that it would meet in about a week or two, until I discovered that the notice was inserted only as a matter of form to be changed later. Why do we need these lengthy proclamations with all the titles and everything else inserted only to discover that what is being announced is a matter of very minor importance.
It is a change from potatoes to radishes-a miracle.

That is all. I cannot see why all this preliminary material could not be inserted in the gazette once-if that is essential-and after that the statement could be made in a form in which we could readily find it. I have under my hand a page of the gazette; I do not think I need take up the time of the committee in reading it, but it is an astonishing production. speechtext: There is a motion before the chair to reduce the item to the amount of one dollar.

Explain the motion.
Mr. POW'ER: I do not know that there is any particular necessity to explain it, because I think it speaks for itself. My views are well known to former members of tha house. My motion is to reduce the estimate for the salaries of the Civil Service Commission, amounting to $239,000 odd, to one dollar. In so moving I am animated partly by my own convictions on the matter, which, as I have already said, are well known to the house, and partly because of my ardent desire to assist some of my hon. friends opposite in what I know is a project they have greatly at heart. In my own constituency there is a large number, perhaps sometimes too large, of very staunch supporters of the polities of hon. gentlemen opposite. Some of them have been kind enough on occasions to vote for me. Others did not do so, but I respect them for the views which they hold and for the tenacity with which they hold them. A great many of these people deserve much from the party which is now in power, and no one would be more pleased than myself-I am absolutely sincere and quite serious when I say this-to see these men who year in and year out have rendered stalwart service to the Conservative party now obtain some kind of reward therefor. But they are being debarred from the recognition to which they are entitled by an iniqui-

Supply-Civil Service Commission
tous piece of legislation known as the Civil Service Act. Hon. gentlemen opposite know this perhaps far better than I do, that the newspapers would support them in abolishing the Civil Service Act. Hon. gentlemen opposite themselves in public addresses on numerous occasions have said that whenever the opportunity presented itself they would do whatever lay in their power to abolish the Civil Service Act and do away with the Civil Service Commission. It would perhaps not be possible for me to quote at any great length some of the addresses which have been made on this subject, but I have before me a copy of a letter which appeared in a newspaper, Le Journal, published in the city of Quebec, in its edition of May 2, 1931. As hon. gentlemen opposite know, Le Journal is the official organ of the Conservative party and of the government in the city and district of Quebec. In case the hon. members who sit on the front benches opposite may not have seen this letter, which is addressed to them, parhaps I may be permitted to translate a few paragraphs.
What is the date of the letter?
It appears in Le Journal of May 2, 1931. The letter is signed "A.G." I have no doubt that "A.G." is well known to a number of my hon. friends opposite.
Perhaps it is Gagnon.
No, because the initials of my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) are O.G. It is an open letter addressed to the federal ministers. I shall endeavour to translate it as I go along.
You may qualify for a position as translator.

Perhaps if some of the members of the commission hear me, they may give me a position as a translator here in parliament, and I shall have the pleasure not only of listening to but of translating some of the remarks of my hon. friends opposite, and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that it would be no mean task in many cases. The letter reads:
I take the liberty of drawing your earnest attention to a state of affairs which I think is most serious. I do it with all the deference which is due to you, but with all the insistence which the serious nature of the subject demands. The people of this province were for a long time under the impression that the exercise of authority in this country had been confided only to members, senators and the representatives of the crown, acting separately or together, as is provided in the British North America Act, but for several years past, and especially for several months past, the people have been asking themselves if the so-called democratic regime is in force in this country.
This is addressed to the federal ministers on May 2, 1931.
Manifestly the influence of the representatives of the people chosen in each electoral division no longer counts in the councils of the nation-councils which the constitution did not provide for and of which the people are ignorant, of whose jurisdiction the people are ignorant, and who for a reason of which the people have not been informed administer this or that service with a lack of intelligence and a stupidity known only to glorified plutocrats in all their power and glory. More often than not they are worn out politicians. These irresponsible commissions decide, settle, name, dismiss, legislate and administer as if they were appointed by divine right. The elected of the people have no right to control, no right to reprimand, no right to advise, no right to blame them. These oligarchic bodies have become the dispenser of the administrative authority-
And so on. The article continues:
The Civil Service Commission nominated to public employment your opponent in the last election and you have not a word to say about it.
I do not know that that really happened; I think that probably the newspaper has been exaggerating. I continue my translation:
It pays no attention to your recommendations. It and its sister commission, the railway commission, know more, or are assumed to know more, than you and all the other members of parliament representing the province of Quebec through its urban and rural constituencies. You cannot advise those commissions, you cannot make representations to them. But the people do not understand the situation, because that which is absurd is repugnant to their ordinary common sense.
Addressing the minister the article continues:
You cannot eternally ignore popular discontent. No regime, no party, can live very long if it has to carry with it cannon balls such as are these anti-democratic commissions. The province of Quebec, particularly the district of Quebec, complaints, and rightly so. of these commissions and does not understand why you do not bring order out of this present absurd situation. Your own electors are displeased and discontented and do not hesitate to tell it to you. Do you wish to commit suicide?
That sounds very much like "perishing in the attempt."
Do you wish to leave to your successors-
This from a Tory paper!
Do you wish to leave to your successors the great merit of having rid the country of these dictators who irritate it so much? Perhaps you do not quite understand the situation. Go through the constituencies, interrogate your electors, ask your leaders in the parishes what they think of it, and you will soon learn what the situation is. Do not forget that on Quebec your future depends. Do not allow these irresponsible adversaries to take Quebec away from you.

I see he is ready and I hope he will give me his hearty support.
With pleasure.

I am glad to hear him say so. It will not be necessary for him to mention, as he did in the observations which he made in his own county last Sunday, that he had made a speech of forty minutes and it had taken the leader of the opposition four and a half hours to answer it.
I deny absolutely having uttered such words, Mr. Chairman.
I am awfully sorry to hear the denial, for the statement was so good.
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw his statement. [DOT]	.

I withdraw the statement
with great pleasure, and accept the denial of the hon. member for Dorchester that he did not say it had taken the leader of the opposition four and a half hours to answer his forty minute speech. I do that gladly and with all deference to my hon. friend from Dorchester. Now I think he owes it to his electors, and at any rate to his colleagues on the government side-for I know he is ready to fulfil his obligations and promises,- to join me in an endeavour to rid the country of this infamous and nefarious institution.

Mr. Chairman, I did not
think this question would be raised this evening because yesterday I understood that other business would occupy our attention today, and therefore I am not prepared to speak at length on this matter. I think my hon. friend from Quebec South will pay me the compliment-although I do not deserve many

-that I do not lack courage. Therefore I am absolutely pleased to say that I share his views about the Civil Service Commission. However I cannot vote for his amendment, because I think by its adoption that we should arrive at no practical results, but deprive the civil servants of their wages. My hon. friend and myself are certainly not antagonistic to civil servants, as civil servants, but we are to a certain degree opposed to the present system. I have been described, justly or unjustly, as being an enemy of the Civil Service Commission. I am not an enemy of the Civil Service Commission so far as the principle of promotion by merit is concerned, but I am against the actual organization and administration of the commission. Those who in 1917 proposed the creation of a Civil Service Commission stated that its purpose was to apply the merit system in making appointments to the civil service; but, as has been said so often in this house and outside, the activities of the commission appear to be based on an entirely different principle. May I quote to the committee an interesting article which appeared shortly after the July election in the Mail and Empire? It is signed by a very distinguished educationist, Doctor W. L. Grant, principal of Upper Canada College, Toronto. He suggests that the act should be amended and refers to what has taken place since 1917, and he mentions that my hon. friend from Quebec South wished to have the Civil Service Commission abolished. If I recollect rightly, the hon. member moved a motion for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission. Unfortunately for him this motion was referred to a special committee, which sat for about fifteen days. I have before me the long report which was printed later, and I do not see that any practical results were attained. Nevertheless I will refer to it, because some interesting expressions of opinion were given. A great number of distinguished men who appeared as witnesses before the committee stated that the Civil Service Commission ought to be reorganized, and among those witnesses was Mr. New-combe, at that time deputy minister of justice, and now one of the most eminent judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. I am sure a great many members of the house will attach much importance to what he said, so I would refer hon. members to the report of the proceedings of the special committee appointed to inquire into the operation of chapter 12, 8-9, George V, reading from page 678. Mr. Drummond put the following question:

Supply-Civil Service Commission
While improvements could be made in the working of the Civil Service Commission, do you approve of the Civil Service Commission as a means to that end, or to the desired end?
And Mr. Newcombe answered:
What I said was that I thought the Civil Service Commission could serve a useful purpose in ascertaining qualifications for clerical positions, so that there would be a body to whom we could refer, who would be able to certify to employees who had capacity in one line or another, according to the nature of the work required. But when you go above that and ask them to make selections for professional, technical or special positions, I say that that service could be performed better, with more economy, and produce better efficiency without the assistance of a commission.
I think a great many members of the house will agree with that gentleman; what he said is absolutely correct. If the Civil Service Commission were only a body having as its principal objective the organizing of examinations to make applicants qualify, it would be all right, but the powers which were given that commission in 1917 and which have been continued by the Liberal government are absolutely extraordinary. They are tantamount to the destruction of responsible government because, as the hon. member has .said with more eloquence than I have at my command, they deprive the ministers and the members from making appointments. I would not be so much against the commission if at least it had power to make appointments, but they do not always do so. Sometimes they hold examinations and the gentleman who succeeds is not appointed; in many instances the commissioners, after having established an eligible list, send that list to an official in the department and ask this official to make the appointment. Why, Mr. Chairman, I cannot conceive that a more ridiculous system might exist, because if a minister cannot judge the merits of a candidate, why should a subordinate official, who sometimes holds an unimportant position, be entitled to make an appointment? It is absolutely ridiculous.
Therefore I suggest that this commission should be reorganized. Really I do not want to be looked upon as desiring publicity in the matter, because everything I could say was said in 1922 by my hon. friend from Quebec South. I am only repeating what he said, in less eloquent terms, but I ask this house why they did not go the limit in 1923.
I sincerely regret, Mr. Chairman, that a moment ago the hon. member for Quebec South deemed it wise to put a little political flavour into his words, because I think this matter should be considered from a nonpolitical standpoint. However, since he thought it well to bring politics into his expressions, 22110-190
I might quote what Doctor Grant said with regard to what the Liberal party did in 1923, after the hon. member had brought his motion before the house. I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee, so I will only say that Doctor Grant said that all that the Liberal party did was to appoint two men, one a second hand journalist from Toronto and the other a shop-worn secretary to the former Minister of Justice. I do not want to say anything about those gentlemen; I have nothing against them, but justly or unjustly they are looked upon in the province of Quebec as being the agents of the Liberal party. I do not want to be unjust; I only repeat what is said in and out of the house, and I think the members of the Civil Service Commission should be absolutely above suspicion.
Therefore I think, Mr. Chairman, that an inquiry should be held. There is a further reason, which is well known to all hon. members of this house. During January of this year complaints were laid in the criminal courts of Ontario against two inspectors of the Civil Service Commission. These complaints were to the effect that a great many employees in the post office at Montreal had been given positions because they had handed sums of money, in some cases amounting to over $500, to these inspectors. Although the charges have been dismissed by the criminal courts of Ontario, other charges are pending. When those charges were made against Bouchard and Chartrand there was a great outcry not only in the province of Quebec but in the province of Ontario as well, and public opinion demands that an investigation takes place immediately. As the hon. member for La-belle stated a few days ago, I have more or less confidence in parliamentary inquiries, and I think a royal commission should be appointed for this purpose.
I do not think I would serve any useful purpose if I spoke at greater length, but I will vote against the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec South because, as I have said, no good result would be obtained. I say this, however, Mr. Chairman:	I will
certainly continue to hold the view that the Civil Service Commission should be, if not abolished, at least reorganized on a different footing. I know that at this stage of the session it is rather late to make a motion to that effect, but I promise the hon. member for Quebec South that if nothing is done in the meantime, next year-and I hope he will support my humble remarks-I will make a motion calling for an investigation and the reorganisation of the commission.

I can quite sympathize
with the hon. member whom we have just heard. He is a newcomer to this house, and I have no doubt he went through his election in the ordinary way. When he found that his party had been returned to power he expected that probably he would get more in the way of patronage than apparently he has been able to secure so far. However, I am surprised at some of his remarks; I refer especially to the statement that in certain cases, after examinations were Reid, the names of the candidates were submitted to minor officials in some departments and that these officials were asked to pass upon them. The hon. member said that was a ridiculous system. I I agree with him; that is a ridiculous system, but it never obtained under former governments.
Oh, oh.

I mean what I say. I
do not think hon. members opposite can quote one instance where an appointment has been referred by the commission to a minor official in any department in this city. If that has happened since my hon. friend was elected, then he should direct his criticism not against the act, which does not allow any such thing, but against whatever department or whatever minister has allowed that to take place. Under the act, when an appointment is made the department may reject the candidate who has been appointed; but it then becomes the duty of the commission to suggest another. And the decision always rests with the commission. If it has come to the attention of my hon. friend that some minor official in one of the departments has taken upon himself the responsibility of making an appointment, surely he should give the particulars to the house, for that is contrary to the act and it should be dealt with accordingly.
My hon. friend made reference to an inquiry held some ten years ago, I believe, by a special committee of the house, on a motion of the hon. member for Quebec South. I was one of the members of the committee and, as I distinctly recall, the evidence given was of a very diversified character. It is true that, as my hon. friend indicated a moment ago, Mr. Newcombe expressed an opinion to a certain purport. But the evidence was so conflicting-perhaps my hon. friend has read some of it-as to make it a very difficult task for the committee to accept any decisions based upon it. I remember in a general way that the deputy ministers objected to the commission having any influence in the matter of promotions, while the evidence that came from outside indicated an objection to
fMr. Gagnon]
the commission having any definite influence with respect to appointments. In other words, there was considerable opposition from the witnesses on both sides, both in regard to appointments and in regard to the promotion system. I must say, in all fairness, that the report of that committee was rather in the nature of a compromise. I will not admit that it did reflect to the fullest degree the evidence that was submitted.
As for the commissioners, I am sure my hon. friend opposite will not emphasize the remarks he has made-or rather the implication-without endorsing that statement with reference to either Dr. MacTavish or Mr. Tremblay. We might with equal propriety remind the committee that the chairman of the commission is a former Conservative minister. But we do not find fault with Dr. Roche, and I think hon. members opposite should show the same consideration and refrain from casting any aspersions on men of such high and distinguished character as Dr. MacTavish and Mr. Tremblay. Those gentlemen have a very difficult task to perform. On certain matters the commission decides by unanimous vote, and it never oocurred to any of us in such cases to insinuate that the chairman of the commission, as a former Conservative, had been led astray by his previous principles.
I did not in any way attack either Dr. MacTavish or Mr. Tremblay. I said that Mr. Grant had made, in an article in the Mail and Empire, the statement to which I referred.

My hon. friend did not make the statement direct, but he left an inference. It would have been more frank for him to have made the statement himself if he did not see fit to ignore it. It seems to me that if we get into a debate of that kind we can just as properly find fault with the chairman of the commission. But we are not trying to do anything of the sort.
I agree with my hon. friend that the charges brought against certain examiners under the commission are very grave, and I am not satisfied myself with the decision arrived at so far. I am certainly strongly in favour of a full inquiry in cases of that kind. I know that when we were in power candidates were told time and time again that they must subject themselves to examination, inasmuch as the system was based on merit; and when they fail to qualify in examinations they must certainly have a feeling of resentment when they find out that in certain cases the examinations, possibly, have not been on the level.
