I suggest that it would be well for us to have in this house some time a non-partisan discussion with reference to the commission. Frankly, I congratulate my hon. friend from Quebec South on the stand he has taken. No attempt on the part of ministers to amend the Civil Service Aot to serve their own purposes has ever met with much favour from an opposition, whether Conservative or Liberal. That has been the experience of the house in the past. When a member gets into opposition he is not so anxious to have the Civil Service Act properly amended as he is to see the newcomers in the same position in which he found himself when his party was in power. For that reason I congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South. He has nothing to expect-I hope he has not made a compact with them-
Not yet.

He has nothing to expect from the abolition of the Civil Service Commission, but he stands by what he thinks is right. I think, however, that if we were to have a discussion on the Civil Service Commission it would be better to have that discussion on a bill repealing the act than in connection with the estimates. Certainly it is obvious that so long as the commission exists it is necessary to vote the money to enable it to carry on. The amendment moved by my hon. friend affords an opportunity for hon. members to affirm their principles, but personally I should feel embarrassed if I voted to-night against the provision of salaries and contingencies needed by the commission. I will take this course, however-and this may be a way of not pronouncing too strongly on either side. There is certainly ground for this parliament discussing the matter fully, and I hope that, if not in this debate, then on some other occasion, the whole subject will be taken into consideration in an entirely nonpartisan spirit. In the meantime, the amendment is before the committee and it may receive support from either side. And for Once,-while I am not a strong partisan of the commission, at the same time I feel that if they are to live they must be paid their salaries and contingencies-I will avail myself of the privilege claimed earlier in the session by the hon. member for Labelle and refrain from voting on the amendment either way.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	The hon. member has
made an excellent speech but I must confess that he has not shed very much light on the subject. Perhaps I lack intelligence, but I do not know yet whether the hon. gentleman is

or is not in favour of the commission; I do not know whether his opinion has changed since he has crossed the floor or whether he still holds to the views he held when in power.
I am not supposed to be a frenzied democrat, but I will put this question frankly to my hon. friend from St. James, who is an experienced member and was at one time a distinguished minister: Does not the Civil Service Commission represent the abolition of responsible government? Does it not represent the abolition of democratic government in Canada? Here is an autocratic body absolutely independent of parliament and of the minister who is responsible. He has to answer to the house. I fail to see-probably it is my old Liberal blood boiling up; it comes to the surface sometimes if only to remind hon. members opposite of Liberal principles-why this Civil Service Commission should exercise so much power without the consent of this parliament, without any responsibility to this parliament. They can take action, they can spend public money and endanger the exchequer of this country without having to answer to anyone. As far as I am concerned I think it is an antiquated theory to believe in a body of this kind. The question is whether or not we in this house are going to support-I was going to say a "Torified" institution, but my hon. friends would not admit that-an antiquated institution very much like the Soviet government. This body is above the people, it spends the people's money and is not responsible to the people. I will not use the word in a political sense, but I am too much of a Conservative to admit a doctrine of that kind. We are here to protect the rights of the people, and for the honour of the country and the good of the people I think that that commission should disappear, and the sooner it disappears the better it will be.

Mr. Chairman, on this occasion I find myself differing from the hon. member who has moved the motion (Mr. Power). I had nine years' experience in administering a very large department under the workings of the Civil Service Act. I do not for one moment maintain that that act is perfect-I think it could be amended and be made much more beneficial- but what do my hon. friends want to do? They want to abolish the act of parliament which creates the commission. Parliament took full responsibility for passing that act and putting it on the statute book, and the act is the authority under which the commission operates. If the act needs amending, let someone move the amendments so that

Supply-Civil Service Commission
we can discuss them. I remember quite well that when this matter was up before many hon. members on this side were of the opinion that it would be better to revert to the patronage system. I do not see that there is any disadvantage in a civil service commission choosing and appointing as it does under the provisions of the act, and in having people enter the service approved by regulations. That system is just as good as the one which prevailed previously, under which recommendations were made by hon. members for partisan service to them or to their party. I can see very little difference in the two systems, in fact I see some improvement in the former. I know that many of my hon. friends oppose very vigorously the operation of the Civil Service Act, and I know that many hon. gentlemen opposite would like to be in a position to make recommendations to the ministers of the various departments with respect to appointments, but I do not think the service would be improved by such a practice. In my opinion many changes could be made in the act to make it more workable, but that is not what my hon. friends are after. They are after the control of appointments to the civil service. There is no camouflage about that. I suppose we all would like that power in order to reward those who work hard for us; we would like to do that sort of thing, but on the other hand I do not think the service would be improved.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Has there been a marked improvement in the civil service since the commission came into being?

I did not have the honour of presiding over a department prior to the advent of the Civil Service Commission, but I did have to deal very largely with civil servants, and I found them in most cases to be very efficient. In many cases those civil servants had not received their appointments through the Civil Service Commission, but they were good civil servants. I have no complaint to make at all; I received the most courteous treatment. Thousands of leases of various kinds were dealt with by the civil servants in the Department of the Interior, and I can say that in the nine years I had charge of that department we did not have a single case in which it could be proved that partisanship was shown in any decision made by a civil servant. As I said before, many of these civil servants were in the service before the commission was formed, but since that time all appointments, with the exception of a few, have been made by the commission. I for one would not wish to revert to the practice

of having appointments made on a partisanship basis, and I take that stand rather firmly. At any time it is proposed to abolish the act in its entirety and revert to partisanship appointments, I wTill oppose such a move, much as I should like to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec South.

May I refer the committee to the report of the special committee of the Senate on the civil service, which sat in 1924 and was presided over by the Hon. F. L. Beique. The following appears on page 9 of its report:
Your committee therefore recommends-
(1) That when a vacancy occurs in the public service by reason of death, resignation or otherwise, such vacancy be not filled by promotion or otherwise except on report of the Civil Service Commission after consultation with the minister or deputy minister. In case of disagreement the facts should be referred to the governor in council for decision, and a report should be made to parliament respecting all such decisions with the reasons therefor.
I quote this report of that committee to show that some improvement could be made, and I think the suggestion made by .the committee is very reasonable. This house could act upon that suggestion and make some amendments to the act. I make that statement to show that we on this side of the house who appear to be more or less against the Civil Service Commission do not want to return to the partisan system of appointments; we want only to amend the act in order that it may be consistent with the principles of responsible government. This suggestion is that although the Civil Service Commission have the right to fill vacancies it should do so only after conferring with the minister or the deputy minister in order to choose the appointee. As matters now stand, examinations are held and appointments made, and in most cases the commissioners never have an opportunity of seeing the candidates. During the regime of my hon. friends opposite, an ex-convict was appointed last year to a responsible position. I do not blame my hon. friends, they are not responsible for that, neither is the Civil Service Commission; but such an unfortunate thing would not have happened if the commissioners or the inspectors had been allowed to inquire more fully into the character of the appointees. Therefore I hope an investigation will be made very soon.

There is nothing to prevent the inspectors from inquiring into the qualifications of the applicants. That is one of their instructions.

member for Dorchester refers to those appointments, does he mean the inside or the outside service?

I would be satisfied if the Civil Service Commission were kept for the inside service and abolished with respect to outside service. That would be a great improvement. Of course I understand we cannot have perfection in one day.
With the possible exception of the hon. member for Rimouski, I think I am the only member of this house who has been a civil servant.
Will my hon. friend permit me to state that I was a civil servant in the employ of the Marine department in 1905 and other years.
I was also a civil servant.

It is not my intention to enter into a long discussion of the advantages and disadvantages that accrue from the Civil Service Act. I think we maj7 accept it as a truism that the act can be improved, but the point that I should like to accentuate is this: I think in this regard my experience among the members of the house is unique. I entered the service at a time when a change of government had just taken place. If, Mr. Chairman, you will pardon me the expression, I was a shock absorber for the province of Quebec for the period which succeeded the advent of the Conservative government in 1911. Then to the victor belonged the spoils. I can tell hon. members who would advocate the abolition of the act, possibly without realizing the full responsibility of the result of such a policy were it carried out, that the additional burden that would be thrown upon a member of parliament, especially in these times, did he have to select from his supporters one man for each position for which there might be a thousand applicants, would be such that he should hesitate before going much further in that advocacy. His life would become unbearable. I do not wish to be accused of lecturing the house, as some have been, but even under present conditions the time of members of parliament is largely wasted in bickering about small matters when real and worth while questions are sadly neglected; and if we placed upon the individual member the horrible task of selecting from his supporters those who should fill the civil service, he would have no time to do anything but attempt to square himself with the vast majority who would be dissatisfied.
He would be in parliament only once.

Yes, and he would not
want to be there more than once. I should like to say just a word about the civil service. There are drones in the service; there are drones everywhere, but-and I am not a member for Ottawa-there is in the civil service a large body of hardworking, competent, capable men and women, who rely upon merit for promotion. I think it is only fair that the merit system should be maintained. The Civil Service Act may at times be imperfectly administered, but in its essence it rests on the merit S37stem. It may be that the merit system is not always followed as rigorously and righteously as it should be, but whose fault is that? It is my fault, your fault and the fault of any hon. member who asks the civil service commissioners to do things which they know they cannot or should not do. I merely ask hon. members to give some consideration to these observations, which are the fruit of experience, before they condemn in its entirety legislation which has been on our statute books for some years.
The hon. member for Quebec South is such a good joker that one hardly knows just where his jokes end and his seriousness begins.
I did not hear what the hon. gentleman said. I hope his remark was complimentary.

It seems rather
remarkable that a discussion of this kind can be precipitated at this stage of the proceedings and after the many years that the Civil Service Act has been in operation. I do not intend to go into a lengthy discussion of the desirability of a civil service commission in this country. I had not thought it was necessary to take part in this debate except that those of us who sit in this corner ought at least to register our protest against anything that would in any w7ay interfere with the Civil Service Commission. I quite understand that there are many abuses connected with its actual operation; it may very well be that the Civil Service Commission needs reorganization. It might be we would be better with one civil service commissioner upon whom greater responsibility could be imposed, but

at the same time it would be disastrous if we were to revert to anything like the patronage system. We in this corner protested again and again against the encroachments that took place under the late administration. I cannot at all agree with the idea that in setting up the commission form of administration we are departing from responsible government. Where would one get the individual who would be nonpartisan?
I think that is quite possible.
Oh, oh!

I think it is quite possible to get individuals who would be nonpartisan in their administration of a civil service act, just as we believe that in a great majority of cases we have judges who, although they were partisans before their appointment, after their appointment rise above partisanship and are fairly independent in their administration of justice. .
I agree with the hon. gentleman.
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that the present commissioners are unfair or partisan?
I did not make that suggestion. The hon. member for West Edmonton asked where one could get commissioners who are not partisan.
Does the hon. member :hink the present commissioners are partisan?
I think during the ast ten years that I have been in the house there has been growing up a considerable measure of patronage in connection with the Civil Service Commission.

Patronage by
whom? By the commission?

By the commission. That I would like to see changed and, if necessary, now that we have a change of government I would welcome some reorganiza-
tion of the commission. But I do not think we ought to revert to the patronage system. If I understand aright what has been done in Great Britain over a period of many years, there 'has been developed a very high type of civil servant, and there they have extended their civil service to take in a great many branches which with us are still under the patronage system. They have gradually developed a type of people who have given excellent service in the most responsible positions. I do not despair of my own country. I know that in the pasit we have given over to bitter partisan fights, and I know perfectly well that good many people in this country still have the idea that politics is a game and that the winner has a right to the spoils. But I also believe that there is a younger generation coming up that is getting free from that view of politics, and it seems to me that w'e ought to do everything in our power to assist in the process.
I quite agree with the last speaker that it would be a serious mistake to go back to a system under which each individual member would be expected to give some sort of reward for support. That is to degrade politics and to degrade those who enter into politics. I am very sony that we should have a motion of this kind brought forward, unless it has been done, as I said, partly as a joke, partly to emphasize the need for certain changes. Having been brought forward, however, it has served this purpose; it has served notice on the government that some sort of reorganization within the Civil Service Commission itself is necessary.

May I correct a wrong .impression that is entertained by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat? He has referred to appointments that have been taken out of the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission and placed in the hands of the government. That cannot be done under the act by the government. It can only be done on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission to the government.
Quite so.

But the hon. gentleman
left the impression that that was going on as a matter of patronage and was being done by the government. That is not the case.

Perhaps I did not make myself sufficiently clear. There are two classes, that I had in mind. Some of us remember that some years ago large blocks of employees of this government were taken out from under the commission. I do not

know exactly what pressure was brought by i lie government in order that that should be accomplished.
No pressure.

I have heard rumours to the contrary, and pretty well founded rumours, too. Further, in almost every set of estimates that we have had brought down during the past ten years there have been new appointments created, and it has been stated that the appointment is being made ''notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act." New groups have thus been established which are not under the Civil Service Commission. Those are the two groups to which I referred.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has referred to blocks of employees being taken out of the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. The classes of employees to which he refers were largely in the nature of day labourers and others receiving very small remuneration, and they were for the most part positions of a character that the Civil Service Commission itself found it inadvisable to attempt to advertise and to select appointees for by process of examination. It was recognized that in engaging day labourers and the like for some of the departmental work, nothing was to be gained by the Civil Service Commission setting up an examination for employees of that class, and the Civil Service Commission itself made a recommendation to the government outlining a list of classes of employees who, in their own opinion, it would be much more in the public interest to have appointed, directly by the government, the government being responsible for the appointments, than for the commission itself to attempt to make such appointments.
With respect to the other group which my hon. friend has just mentioned, where appointments are made through the estimates, which contain now and then the mention of some individual's name and his appointment "notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act", in every case where that is done it is on the responsibility of the minister, who gives an explanation to the house why the particular individual should be exempted from the civil service examination, and I think in most cases up to the present the explanation given has been satisfactory. It has been shown that it was in the public interest that the exemption should be made.
I can speak with some degree of certainty of the first class of exemptions because I recollect very well that when the list came to us from the Civil Service Commission at the time we were in office, I was somewhat surprised at its extent, but when I came to look into the class of employees recommended by the commission for exemption from the civil service examination and appointment thereafter by the commission, I began to despair of the Civil Service Commission ever doing anything else if they once began to examine all applicants for those positions.

I should like to inquire from the leader of the opposition if in the finance department whole groups of officers, not one or two at a time, but dozens at a time, were not left outside the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission-in the income tax branch?

The income tax branch was established when my hon. friends were in office, and his government so arranged matters that these employees would not come under the Civil Service Commission. When we came into office those appointments had already been made, and with respect to the income tax branch we simply continued the practice as it had existed under the former administration.
I am not saying anything about who did it. But you said it and kept on repeating it.

It was inevitable, I suppose, that on this vote for salaries for the Civil Service Commission some criticism should be made with respect to its operations. I would suggest to my hon. friend from Quebec South that the amendment having served its purpose as a basis for criticism and argument, it might well now be withdrawn. Parliament having created by statute a Civil Service Commission, and the members of that commission and its employees having been engaged under contract with the government, I cannot conceive that the hon. member for Quebec South would ask this committee by a vote on this item to make an entire breach of contract with the commission and its employees by refusing to make an appropriation exceeding one dollar for their annual services. Parliament, if it is serious at all, cannot take such a position as that.
I wish also to say on behalf of the government that in January last, and from time to time since, it has been represented to the government that some action shoud be taken in view of the alleged revelations made in certain criminal prosecutions now pending, which Concern, possibly, the management, and certainly the operations of the civil service

system. As hon. gentlemen have said, merit is the very essence of the civil service system, but if for merit is to be substituted the payment of bribes to examiners and others, the whole civil service system is brought into grave disrepute. The government so far have taken no active step in the matter of an independent investigation of the charges which have been made. These charges were pending at the time in the courts of Ontario and are now pending in the criminal courts of Quebec, and while those charges were under investigation by the courts and the whole matter was sub judice, it did not seem equitable that such action should be taken by the government. Further than that the government cannot go at present. It would be unfair that we should even take proceedings while these matters are sub judice, but if the charges are sustained I have no doubt the government will feel impelled to make some further independent inquiry, and the results of such inquiry will certainly be brought before parliament for its consideration. In view of that fact I should like to have this vote passed. It mu^t pass. Parliament is in honour bound to pass this vote. It cannot deal with the Civil Service Commission in this indirect, unfair, impassible and impractical way. Therefore I ask that the amendment be defeated and the vote passed.
Out of deference to my hon. friend the Secretary of State I shall be glad to withdraw my amendment if I have the consent of the committee to do so.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: Has the hon. member the consent of the committee to withdraw the amendment?
Carried.

Then I will move another
amendment more in keeping with what the hon. Secretary of State wants. I move that this item be reduced by one dollar.
In this way I am able to meet his wishes. There will not be anything "impractical" or "impossible" about my proposal. The civil servants, that is, those employed by the Civil Service Commission, will be paid. And this amendment will also meet the views of the hon. member for Dorchester. After all, that
[.Mr. Cahan.]
dollar can be made up somewhere else, and I believe I shall be following the proper constitutional practice in seeking to express the views of the house in reference to the principle of any matter which comes before us. Governments have been defeated before now in the old country, if not here, and great principles have been affirmed by a motion to diminish the estimates of any particular branch by one dollar. I believe that any one who is opposed to the principle of a civil service commission should support my amendment. I am prepared here to quote my hon. friend from Dorchester as being absolutely opposed in principle to a civil service commission.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

Surely the hon. gentleman
will not repudiate things before I state them. True, we have had frequent repudiations of newspaper reports and so on, but only after they have been quoted.

I stated my view's a
moment ago and I do not see what purpose my hon. friend can have in quoting other statements of mine.

My hon. friend will
understand that it is somewhat interesting to the committee to know whether the views he expresses in this house are the same as those he expresses in his constituency.
Very, very interesting indeed.

On February 23. 1931, the
hon. gentleman, as reported in another Quebec newspaper, stated:
I denounce in my turn this commission. At the first caucus of the party in Ottawa there will be a question on it. The hon. Mr. Sauve was complaining about it recently and regretted that we, the Conservative members, cannot give any reward to the brave servants of our party.
That is the whole thing in a nutshell.

This is where the matter of
principle is involved:
This law is the negation of the principle of responsible government.
He goes on to say that to-day a minister cannot appoint even a messenger, and so on and so forth. My hon. friend, I think, shares with the hon. member for Montmagny and myself and a number of others in this house, our objection to the principle of a non-responsible body administering any of the affairs of this country. It was on those grounds that in 1923 I moved in this house for the abolition

Supply-Civil Service Commission
of the Civil Service Commission, and afterwards amended the motion to restore the Civil Service Commission to the status it held in the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The matter was referred to a committee, and, as has been well said by the member for Dorchester, nothing came of the committee inquiry. I have some clippings from newspapers of the day. The following from the Montreal Gazette of February 19, 1923, is particularly interesting.
Perhaps the most effective and expeditious remedy for a system of so little value-
Speaking of the Civil Service Commission.
-is to uproot it altogether and throw it aside, which is what Major Power proposes. The Pecksniffs of parliament will receive such a suggestion with hands upraised in pious horror, and they will be quick to impute dubious motives-
I commend that to the Secretary of State.

to those who would lay rude hands upon the sacred ark of civil service reform.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	The member for Winnipeg also.

Perhaps the member for
Winnipeg .might read this, or listen to what I am saying in reference to the question.
The question has always been discussed, more's the pity, in an atmosphere of hypocrisy, although there are many quite sincere men

Including perhaps the member for Winnipeg.
-who think the present act must necessarily be a good thing because it represents what they regard as a good intention. These conditions render a dispassionate discussion of the question almost impossible, and certainly unlikely, yet it is in the last degree desirable that parliament should, in this matter, rid itself of impracticable theories, however exalted, and consider the facts as they are. Those facts stamp the existing system as a failure.
This was in 1923. All down the years since then, although I have not had the same opportunity as to-day, I have continued to oppose the Civil Service Commission because I believe it is the negation of the principle of responsible government. I found it impossible in 1923 to convince the members of the house on my own side, and also members on the other side who then were staunch supporters of the Civil Service Commission because they feared that if there were any loosening in the regulations respecting appointments the party in power would unduly exercise their patronage. But a new house has been created by the last election: there are eighty new members here; the party which was sitting opposite then is now in opposition. That party as a party supported
the Civil Service Commission, although I was one of those who always was opposed to it. I had not the influence, I had not the party standing, I had not the prestige in my party which the hon. member for Dorchester has in his party. He has been on many occasions dubbed the Acting Solicitor General and representative for the district of Quebec.
I deny that.

He cannot deny what the
newspapers have said. Will my hon. friend deny that newspapers have on many occasions called him the Acting Solicitor General?
No paper said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No reputable paper said
that.

I have read that with my
own eyes and my statement is as good as the hon. gentleman's. I have read on several occasions in the newspapers of Quebec that the hon. gentleman was Acting Solicitor General.
Does that make him so?
The point is he has influence with his party. Even now he is sitting in the seat of the Solicitor General.
I sit here only for the purpose of being closer to my hon. friend.
Have you no influence?

I have no influence whatever with hon. gentlemen on that side of the house. But if my hon. friend thinks I have any influence and wishes to increase that influence in the house, he will vote with me when the vote is taken. I am sure if he did so he would be following his own inclinations far more than would be the case if he voted in the opposite way. I know my hon. friend to be honest, frank and candid, probably more so than most mejnbers of the house.
And courageous.

Yes, and courageous, and I am sure he will hesitate a good deal before voting against this amendment. The situation is that there are eighty new members in this house, a large number of them on the other side. They are not tied to the old system of blind submission to the Civil Service Commission, and they have this opportunity of expressing their views against the principle of the Civil Service Commission. I have no interest in moving this resolution except that I hope to see better government come out of the abolition or the reform of the commission.

I believe we have not improved our civil service; I believe there have been far more people taken into the service because of the commission than otherwise would be the case. I believe the expenses have been heavier, and I believe the appointments have not been so good.
Have they been nonpartisan?

Perhaps they have been nonpartisan, but they have not been so good. I do not know whether or not they have been non-partisan; with respect to my own constituency, I never was able to appoint anyone, and I know a large number of hon. members of the house, both on this side and on the other side, who could say the same thing. So why not let us have the courage to stand before our electors and say, "We will take the responsibility for appointments in our constituencies." I was willing to do that when I was a member sitting on the government side, and I am willing to let the defeated candidate in my constituency take the patronage there. I believe his appointments will be better than the appointments made by the Civil Service Commission. He will appoint good Conservatives, and there is no reason why they should not fill civil service positions and fill them well. Half the civil service of Canada, or more-those now in the civil service in the higher positions-were appointed by the Conservatives under the patronage system. I will say this for the civil service of this country: it compares favourably with any in the world, particularly that portion which was appointed before, we went crazy during the war with all kinds of reform, for the most part reactionary movements. I do believe that, this opportunity being given hon. members on both sides of the house, they should say how they feel in this matter and vote against the principle of any civil service commission.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is supposed generally to be expressing the opinions of the people whom he represents. Now we see that the hon. gentleman is moving towards very conservative ground. Perhaps I should not say that, but he appears to be championing the cause of democracy and responsible government. However, the hon. gentleman has defeated himself by his own argument. He said the Civil Service Commission should not be appointed by patronage. I do not know whether he suggests that we should appoint

a new civil service commission every so often, but that commission must be appointed by somebody under the patronage system.
My hon. friend quoted as an example the judges of this country. I think our country compares very favourably with any country in the world, and especially with the republic to our south, in the capacity, the integrity and the high character of our judges, but how are they appointed!? They are appointed under a patronage system and not by the Civil Service Commission, thank God-speaking for our lawyers and for those who plead. Leaving aside the judges, is there one business firm or one business man in this house who would appoint a clerk or any employee under the system followed by the Civil Service Commission, which is forced upon the responsible government of this country? Who is responsible for the appointments; who is responsible for the appointee, for the way he will carry out his work, for his integrity and his character? The minister is responsible, but the minister has nothing to say about the appointment. He has to accept the dictation of an independent, foreign body, over which he has no control and which is responsible to no one except themselves, and unfortunately sometimes to the criminal courts of this country.
I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if this is not a denial of responsible government. If it is not, I do not know what responsible government is. I know of no business firm which would act in this way in regard to the appointment of a clerk, a messenger, or any other employee. We force upon this country, as the hon. member for Quebec South has said, a law which was passed during the war when we were crazy with the abolition of democracy, which I admit is not the way to make war if we desire to win it. As long as we have responsible government; as long as we are responsible to the government, so far as I am concerned I am willing to take my responsibility. I denounced the Civil Service Commission duimg the last election, and I do not deny my words now. What I said before the people I am ready to stand for to-day in the house, and I spoke as a man who believes in responsible government. I said that this commission was the denial of responsible government. I think I was right; I do not think anyone can bring facts to contradict that statement. The best evidence that this system has failed is the fact that, since this law has been in existence, at every opportunity every government has put aside the Civil Service Act and made appointments

Supply-Civil Service Commission
out-side of it in order that they might have employees for whom they were responsible. A further proof is that the civil service was just as good before the appointments were made by the Civil Service Commission, if not better.
Air. AlcGIBBON: I just wish to put myself on record in connection with this question. I was in this house when the measure was passed; I was opposed to it then, and spoke against it, and I have been opposed to it ever since. I am opposed to it now. There is this difficulty, however, which I see and which, to me, is a real difficulty. My objection is largely to the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission in connection with outside appointments. I know nothing about inside appointments, and consequently am not interested in them. However, I do not see how you could abolish the commission at once and leave an army of civil servants here without any person particularly to look after them. Had the hon. member for Quebec South moved 'to take away from the Civil Service Commission all appointments in the outside service, leaving them to the elected member, that proposal would have received my hearty support. I firmly believe, Mr. Chairman, that there is no one more entitled to make appointments than the member elected by the people. The people expect him to do that; he should do it, and I should like to see members of parliament make the appointments no matter upon what side of the house they sit. I do not see how you can do better. It may be said that you will get only .political appointments; that is granted. However, I think along with that you should place this statement, that no matter who the member is, he or she will make the very best appointment possible, according to the judgment of the member. Possibly there might be a better one in some other political ranks; but my claim is this, after many years of public life, that if you can gelt even the second or the third best appointment in your constituency you are doing better than the commission is now doing. AY hat is the commission's procedure? Let us suppose a vacancy occurs in my constituency. If the position involves over $400, I, as a member of the riding, have nothing to do in the matter.
Two hundred.

Four hundred.
Air. A'ENIO 1:	That is, if it is a revenue
office-if the revenue is over $400. But as to salaries generally, all through, it is $200 or
under.
Mr. AlcGIBBON:	That only makes it all
the worse. Now, what happens? They use the machinery of a certain department, like the post office. They send officials to my riding. They do not even consult me. They get their information from a man on the street, or from any other source they please, and they make a report back'to the department. That department forwards it to the commission and the appointment is made, I presume, on that recommendation. These appointments are made by persons who are responsible absolutely to no one. It is on that ground that I base my objection to the act. I say frankly that I am willing to support any day a resolution or a bill that will take the outside service away from the commission. And I have never held any different opinion. I opposed it when the bill was passed in 1918, and I am still opposed to it. It was due, I believe, as the hon. member for Quebec South suggested, to the hysterical effort which was being made during the war to abolish responsible government. We seemed to want to get away from everything in respect to which the people's representatives should be consulted.
I should have been glad had this matter come before the house in a different form. I believe that most hon. members, on either side, are opposed to the commission making outside appointments. I do not believe that the commission itself is anxious for the job. More than that, when you go back to your electors and tell them that you have not a thing to do with it, a large number of them will not believe you. And those that do believe you will say, "You are no good, or you would have something to do with it''. That is an honest statement of fact; I believe it is a fair interpretation of the mind of the electorate. The people expect that the man or the woman whom they elect to represent them in the house will make appointments in their riding. And the member should make them. I shall be glad indeed to support any resolution to that effect. I do not know just how the present amendment will affect the inside service. I do not believe it will affect it at all. If it does not affect it, but leaves it under the commission, I am prepared to vote for the amendment.

I had not intended taking part in this discussion, but in view of the second amendment proposed by the hon. member for Quebec South, I think I had better put myself on record. I do not believe that a discussion of this kind adds very much to the reputation of the. house for seriousness. For two hours we Have been engaging in a debate that will result in nothing. When the

hon. member for Quebec South moved the first ameudment to reduce the amount to one dollar, he knew very well that such a motion would have to be voted down, even by his own friends, because no serious member of this house desires to see civil servants going without their pay. And when he withdraws that amendment and submits the second motion he knows equally well that it can serve no purpose.
I am no great lover of the Civil Service Commission, although I have been on friendly terms with them. As a matter of fact, I have practically no patronage in my county. I cannot find fault with the few appointments that have been made in the county of Compton by the Civil Service Commission, but, in common with many other members, I believe that some changes could be effected for the improvement of the system. When, however, my hon. friend from Quebec South says he wishes to have this house vote on the principle of his motion, I must say that I cannot see the principle involved. As a new member, it is possible that I do not understand or grasp the significance of different motions quite so well as the older members do, but I cannot see where the principle is involved in that motion asking the committee to reduce the vote as the hon. gentleman has proposed. I absolutely fail to see any high principle there at all. If the motion meant anything, if it proposed something definite, then I should be in a position to consider what was involved in it and I should be able to vote either for or against it. But it does not mean anything; it is really only a farce. As I said before, I believe that some changes could be made, but I have no hesitation in declaring that I shall vote against the motion. I believe that every serious member will vote against it, without respect to party politics.

I intend to vote against the amendment. I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South when he moved it. He said it was a negation of the principle of responsible government to hand over to the Civil Service Commission, the engaging of employees. But it seems to me that when he went on to suggest his willingness that the appointments in his constituency should be made by the defeated candidate, that can certainly be regarded as neither more nor less than a negation of responsible government. The hon. gentleman suggests that a man who had been rejected by the people should have the right to make appointments. He might be a man who had failed to obtain the votes of one-fourth of the people living in the constituency, and yet

he would be in a position to make the appointments. That, it seems to me, is too terrible a condition to contemplate at all. The proper way to describe the system which seems to be in favour to-night would be to call it, not the principle of responsible government, but the spoils system.
The deputy speaker said, I believe, that no business concern would think of making appointments of their employees in the way the parliament of Canada makes appointments through the Civil Service Commission. Let me tell him that no business concern would think of running its affairs as we run the business of Canada in this house. They would not think of dividing their forces into two groups corresponding to a government and an opposition. And just because we have this inefficient party system we must resort to the Civil Sendee Commission to make appointments to the. civil service. So far as I am concerned, I do not wish to see even outside appointments removed from the commission. I do not wish to have the responsibility at any time, particularly at a time like this,' of deciding or suggesting who should get appointments. The chief trouble with the Civil Service Commission is that the commissioners are not appointed on the merit system; the appointment is not made because of the fitness or the particular ability of the man to carry out the duties entrusted to him. Such appointments always have been made because of the political affiliations of those who received them. The spoils system starts right at the top. If we want a proper civil service commission and desire to have the civil service properly handled, we. should take care in appointing these commissioners to see that they are fitted for the position. I think that that is all that is needed to ensure a good civil service in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to say that I cannot vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec South, although I concur in many of the views he has expressed, and support in large measure the position he has taken. If the amendment meant what I presume the hon. member intended it to mean, I might vote for it, but I cannot see that it means anything else than a vote of want of confidence in the government, or at least in the minister who presents these estimates. The hon. member for Montmagny put his finger on the situation when he said that no business organization could be carried on under such a system as that under which the Civil Service Commission operates. I will go as far as to say that no such organization or no

Supply-Civil Service Commission
such business could be carried on unless it had behind it the taxpayers of Canada in order to carry the load.
The minister is responsible to parliament, parliament is responsible to the people. The minister is at the head of an organization in connection with which he has no say whatsoever as to who is or is not to be employed to assist in carrying out the responsibilities imposed upon him. The minister has no disciplinary power, and I doubt very much whether the deputy or the assistant deputy has any' disciplinary power. The information I have gathered in discussions with some of the best civil servants we have in this country is to the effect that the power of the minister is confined to sending someone back to the Civil Service Commission to be put in another position. Am I right or am I wrong? I will leave the answer to those who are in a better position than I am to know the facts. Unless it be for an act almost criminal in nature the minister or the deputy minister cannot dismiss a civil servant without referring such dismissal to the Civil Service Commission.
The commission cannot know of the technical duties which these civil servants are called upon to perform. Let me refer for a moment to what the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario has said with regard to the outside service. For example, someone may be required in British Columbia to act as an inspector on a government job costing, say, $100. The engineer in charge of the job and responsible for the work has no say whatsoever as to who shall be placed on that job as inspector.
The hon. member is mistaken there.

It would be hard to
imagine one of the railway companies endeavouring to carry out a certain work and their engineer being compelled to refer to three civilians in the city of Ottawa before he could obtain an inspector for the job. Under our system the elected member who is responsible to the people, or, as has been stated, the defeated candidate, has no say in the appointment; the engineer has no say, and, as every hon. member of this house knows-

Will the hon. member allow me to correct a wrong impression? He has stated that the engineer has nothing to say with regard to the appointment. The resident engineer is the one who holds the examination and after such examination is held, he sends
in his report to the Civil Service Commission as to which of the applicants is the most capable, in his opinion, to fulfil the duties of the position.

My hon. friend may
know what takes place in his constituency, but I know what takes place in mine; I know that the engineer does not hold the examinations in every case.
Who does?
Someone named by the Civil Service Commission.
Not at all.
Oh, yes. I know of a postmaster having been asked to conduct an examination for an inspector on a breakwater dock. The engineer in the district had nothing to say in the matter.

The Minister of Public
Works knows better than that.
That is what is being done, and it follows all the way through.
No, it does not.

I do not blame the
commission; it is the creature of parliament, and I believe it is carrying out its duties and responsibilities as well as it is possible for [DOT] three men situated as they are to do so. I agree with the hon. member for Quebec South that so far as the outside service is concerned the Civil Service Commission is in an impossible position which cannot lead to anything but inefficiency.
So far as the inside service is concerned, it may be all right. I agree that an independent body should make the appointments, but when an appointment is made every promotion, every act of discipline, everything pertaining to the service should be under the control of those responsible for the carrying on of the service. The examining board can say: Jones, Smith or Brown has passed the examination; he has the necessary degree of merit and can fill the position, but those who are responsible for doing the work should say who the appointee is to be, and should be responsible for discipline.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to the spoils system. Perhaps it is a spoils system, but the people expect when they select someone to represent them in the House of Commons, that that individual, whoever he is, or, as the hon. member for Muskoka has said, whoever she is, will represent the opinion of the constituency. If the member does not do that, then, as my hon. friend has said, he is not fit to represent the constituency.

For the sake of his own reputation he will see to it that none but proper persons are appointed He will consult with those who are going to do the work and he will find someone who knows something about it.
Mention was made of the defeated candidate recommending appointments, but that is a negation of responsible government. Responsibility rests upon the ministers of the departments, and they are responsible for accepting recommendations. If they accept a recommendation from a defeated candidate, they are responsible for that recommendation and parliament can hold them responsible.
Reference has been made to the manner of the appointment of the Civil Service Commission. If we retain the commission there is only one way in which it can be appointed. You cannot throw the names of a group of men into parliament to be voted on by hon. members who know nothing about them. The government must make the appointments, unless, as has been said before, you set up a sort of super-commission to appoint the Civil Service Commission, and in that case, who is going to appoint the super-commission? If my hon. friend at some future time will bring in a resolution or a bill, if you will, to amend the Civil Service Act so as to put it on a sound basis so far as an examining body is concerned, I shall support him if I am in the house at the time.

I am through with the
estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State, and my memorandum which I had at hand last night I have not here now, but if the right hon. member will leave that as a question I shall certainly take advantage of an early opportunity to explain it fully to him, because I am sure there is a fair explanation.

I perhaps
should apologize to my hon. friend for suggesting the question out of the proper order, and he is quite right in saying that the ques-

tion should have been asked last night, but I am asking it now, not in relation to salaries, but rather in regard to the way in which the Civil Service Commission seems to operate on occasions. I have noticed-I am not speaking now of my hon. friend's administration, but in the past when responsibility was more on my shoulders than it is at the moment-that in some way or another one minister seemed to be able to get any number of principal clerks appointed and another minister did not seem able to get any; and also that not infrequently there were relatively many promotions that affected individuals at the top, while the great body of the service continued to remain in pretty much the same position.
I can assure the hon. member that no one in any branch of the department over which I have the honour to preside has been promoted or demoted at my instance.

I know that,
and that gives point to what I have been saying. The hon. Secretary of State has just borne out the point I was trying to make. My hon. friend says that no one in his department has been promoted or demoted at his instance, yet the estimates before us today, and which the minister has asked the committee to pass, show that in his department last year there were five principal clerks and this year there are eight principal clerks, and those additional three appointments or promotions have been made, not by the minister responsible to parliament but by the Civil Service Commission. That is the kind of thing which I think is irritating a good many who speak in the name of responsible government. Where is the responsibility of the government when you have a minister obliged to accept promotions whether they meet with his own view or not of what is essential in the service of his own particular department?

If the right hon.
leader of the opposition will bear with me, I think he is making a mistake. No promotion can possibly be made in the department unless it has first been requested by the department of the Civil Service Commission. The promotion is made by the Civil Service Commission, but it is first requested by the department itself.

I am obliged to my hon. friend for drawing my attention to that fact. That is an additional feature. There has to be, as I recollect it, some repre-

Supply-Secretary oj State
sentation made by the department to the Civil Service Commission as to the necessity for additional clerks. The recommendation in this Case may have been made to the Civil Service Commission by the deputy minister or someone else in the department, if the law governing the commission has, as I assume it has, been complied with. But one thing is certain from what the minister has told us himself, and that is that he as a minister has not had any knowledge of the fact that three additional principal clerks have been added to the department in the time that he has been in office. That is an illustration of the sort of thing that goes on in connection with the work of the Civil Service Commission, and it is that sort of thing which I believe has exasperated many members who as members feel a certain responsibility which, however they do not enjoy, for appointments that are made, whether they be new appointments or promotions^
Having said that much by way of criticism as to the extent of the application of the principle, and as to the unnecessary lengths to which it seems to me it has gone, I wish again to repeat that as to the principle itself of the Civil Service Commission, I could not support any vote that sought to have the principle denied. I would wish to see the principle maintained but carried out more in accord with the will and wish of the members of the House of Commons.

The minister of the crown who presents the estimates for the Civil Service Commission is by practice the Secretary of State. The Civil Service Commission itself is very independent. This prevents a minister assuming political responsibility fully with respect to it. The government, however, have presented these estimates, which are the ordinary estimates, and- we must see that this vote is passed if it is possible to pass it. We regard the discussion as very valuable indeed, but the motion to reduce the item by one dollar is a ridiculous motion, it seems to me.
The hon. gentleman is too fond of using the term ridiculous in regard to other people. No man has made himself more ridiculous in this house than the hon. gentleman himself yesterday and to-day.

I am speaking of the motion to reduce the vote. The remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition must have very great weight with the government of the day in connection with any review of the Civil Service Act. The Civil Service Act must not be sustained simply by one party or the other. Amendments to that act must be arrived at,

not by unanimous consent, but by the general consent of the house. That act, if it is to continue, must have the general approval of the house, and therefore it seems to me it must be the bounden duty of the government of the day to take into very serious consideration the representations which the right hon. leader of the opposition and other members of the house have made to-night. But that fact being recognized, I do trust that members of the house will vote down this amendment and support the vote in its original form.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 17; nays, 69.

Before the motion carries,
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the attention of the committee to the fact that a number of members did not vote. For instance, I noticed that the member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) was in his seat and did not vote one way or the other on the resolution; I think the member for Lake St. John (Mr. Duguay) did not vote; and a number of other members who have expressed their views on the Civil Service Commission similar to mine did not vote. I am very glad to notice that and I suppose they will have some explanation to give to their electors, to whom they declared they would do their very best when the time came to support their demands for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission.

Item agreed to.
Public printing and stationery-printing, binding, etc., the annual statutes, $16,000.

I notice that the statutes passed at the special session last September are available in the form of a small booklet. I would suggest to the Secretary of State that he consider the binding of these statutes with those of the present session in order that they may be kept in regular form.
I will make that representation to the printing bureau. My hon. friend will notice that the vote is slightly increased by reason of the printing of the statutes for the special session.
Has the minister particulars of the revenue received for public printing and stationery?

There is a very considerable revenue, for instance, from the statutes. This vote is simply for the purpose of paying the cost, but the revenue is paid directly into the consolidated revenue fund to the credit of the Receiver General. I have not all the details, but I can give the hon. member some particulars on the next vote.

money is collected from every department of the government for printing. That is revenue.

A distinction must be
made between the revenue derived from the departments and from the public. For instance, we sell a certain number of statutes to the public direct, and the printing bureau gets the money; we also get revenue from the public on account of the Canada Gazette. 1 think the ex-Postmaster General is referring to the amounts paid by every department to the printing bureau for printing work performed for them.

That runs up into tens of
thousands of dollars. I have not the particulars at hand to-night.

Perhaps the Secretary of
State would undertake to give those particulars to me.
With great pleasure.

One of my reasons for asking for these particulars is that the Post Office Department gets no credit for the franking it does for the House of Commons, the Senate and the various departments, amounting to over $1,000,000 a year; but if it wants any printing done it has to pay the printing bureau.
Quite so.

I have always thought that the Post Office Department should get credit for every bit of work done for the other departments. The king's printer gets credit for all the printing he does for the various departments-
Otherwise we would have no money to carry on our work.

-the customs department
gets credit for every dutiable article that comes in for the other departments, the railway department gets credit for all the transportation it does for the other departments; but the Post Office Department gets no credit for the work it does for the other departments amounting, as I have said, to over $1,000,000 a year. I do not think it is fair to that large department that it should not at least get book credit for such work.

Item agreed to.

Printing and binding government publications for sale and distribution to departments and the public, $40,000.
Will the minister tell the committee whether there is any revenue under this item?

Yes, last year there was a revenue in excess of expenditure of some $28,000, I believe, but that goes into the consolidated revenue fund. We do not credit the revenue coming from this work; the appropriation is made by parliament and the proceeds coming from the work done goes into the consolidated revenue fund.
Will the minister tell the committee whether the expenses involved in these items we are now passing are met by the revenue? What is the total revenue of the department?

I cannot give that at the
moment.
A short time ago I asked that question, and the minister said he would look it up and let me have the information.

I promised to give that information. As a matter of fact really the operation of the department costs the treasury less than $80,000 a year. I have discussed this question with the officials, and we think we do some things too cheaply. For instance, we think the rates for advertising in the Canada Gazette should be a little higher in order to keep them in line with other advertising rates. We are hoping during the present year to make some reduction of that cost of $80,000.

When the minister says the department costs $80,000 a year I suppose he takes into consideration the payments made by the different departments for work done; when all these payments are made and when the revenue is collected from other sources, there is a deficit of about $80,000 with regard to the printing bureau?

Something like that, and if we were paid for everything we did we would show a very considerable surplus, because the amount of work done in various forms for other departments and for parliament itself is very great. I think the service rendered is efficient, and it is rendered at low cost.

Before we pass the last item in connection with the printing bureau I should like to make one remark. It seems that we ex-ministers are rather monopolizing the committee to-night, but it was brought to my attention many times-though I will admit no action resulted-that the estimates of the

Supply-Immigration
printing bureau are submitted in a very peculiar way. If you look at page 101, which contains the details of civil government, you will find only thirty-two employees mentioned. These constitute the executive staff of the printing bureau. It is a well known fact that there are over 800 employees, workmen of different classes, in that bureau, and their salaries, together with the cost of the material used and the general overhead expenses, are paid not from a vote of this house but from the accumulation of votes for printing spread over the different departments. In the archives branch, for instance, you will find a certain amount for printing, and that is so in connection with the Department of Public Works and other departments of the government. These cumulative estimates make up a formidable amount, which goes to pay for the work done by the printing bureau and the salaries of those eight hundred employees. It has been submitted that it might be more proper to have an estimate submitted which would include all those employees actually in the employ of the department.
I am sorry my hon. friend did not do that when he was in office.

It was brought to my attention during the course of my administration, and I must say there was something appealing in it, but the objection was that it would mean a considerable departure from what we had done so far. However, I was going to ask the present Secretary of State whether the same matter has been brought to his attention and whether he has not something to say about it.
Mr. CAHAN; My hon. friend knows that the employees are paid the rates of wages current in Montreal and Toronto, and they are paid out of the revenues of the department. We nave now 720 employees in that department, and the salaries last year amounted to $1,276,517, which amount was paid out of the revenues of the department.

That is to say, there is a special act governing the printing bureau whereby an advance of $750,000 is made to the king's printer in order to carry on the work for the different departments. Previously it was $500,000, and the amount was increased to $750,000.

I may tell my hon. friend that when I came into the department I found owing, at the time it was brought to my attention sometime in December, some $850,000 by the different departments. Later that amount was reduced to about $5,000, so that I think I am a pretty good bill collector.

I was trying to explain the system under which the printing bureau operates, and I wanted to ask my hon. friend whether representations have been made to him, as they were to me, that the estimates of that department should be brought down in a different way in order to show the full number of workmen and other employees in the bureau instead of having separate amounts voted for printing in the different departments. If, instead of voting $15,000 in one case, $20,000 in another case and so on, without any explanation being available, the printing bureau would submit estimates covering all those working in that department, it would give the house a better picture of what is taking place. If my hon. friend tells me that he has not done it, and I say the preceding government did not do it, that will be the end of it, but I know these representations received consideration by the former government and I take this first opportunity of bringing them to the attention of my hon. friend and asking him if he has given consideration to the suggestion.

Yes, I have gone very carefully into every detail of expenditure and: revenue in connection with that department.
I am accustomed to accounts, and I brought the matter referred to by my hon. friend to>
the attention of the Prime Minister, who is Minister of Finance of the day. The final decision was delayed pending the reconstruction of a branch of the finance department by a bill which has been brought down. A new system of accounting is to be inaugurated, I believe, for all departments, and when that matter comes up again I shall have great pleasure in renewing that representation with the Prime Minister.

I think this would be an excellent opportunity for the minister to tell the people and the country what the outlook for his department is for the next three years. What will be the policy of the department in connection with immigration? I ask for a statement in this regard for the reason that, apart from one or two commercial institutions in the United States that seem to be over-optimistic, the general forecast is that the present depression is likely to endure for some time. I assume the minister does not contemplate the reopening of this country to an inflow of immigration, and I should like to know the position he takes in regard to the present personnel of his department. Is he going to maintain the entire overhead required for the carrying on of a full policy or will there 'be a reduction in keeping with the almost total abolition of the immigration service?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
With respect to what the hon. member for Bow River has just said, I can assure the members of this committee- probably at the risk of not following the time-honoured course of announcing beforehand what a policy may or may not be-that as long as conditions in this country are as they are to-day there need be no fear that the bars will be let down to immigrants. We have problems enough on our hands because of, let me say, the thoughtless or undisciplined migrations into this country in the past. I am not going to charge those who immet-diately preceded us in government with any delinquency in that regard-that probably could be just as successfully charged against those who in turn preceded them. I think the * hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) and myself are in a measure crusaders so far as the rigidity of the present policy is concerned. He identified the problem before I did, but I identified it some, two or three years ago. As I saw it, we were not taking the care we should take in introducing people into this

Supply-Immigration
country or in encouraging them to come; we were not sure that they were being assimilated. I do not want to charge the late government with that because I think everyone in this country, in government and out of government, has been just a little thoughtless as to what problem was being created with respect to the encouragement of immigration.
The hon. member for Bow River asks about the curtailment of the present vote. This vote is not likely to be reduced in the next two or three years because the experience gained in presiding over the department since last August has taught me that it is a great deal easier to admit people into a country than it is to keep them out. This vote will have to be maintained in a large measure in connection with the preventive service and the survey of those who seek admission into Canada. I can see no immediate hope for any considerable reduction.
So far as this government is concerned, and I think I can speak with a good deal of confidence in connection with the matter, the question of immigration into Canada will not in the future be a matter of politics. If in the past politics has entered into this question, we have learned our lesson and the depression which is at present upon us has made manifest the mistakes which were made in the past. In future immigration will be entirely dissociated from politics and will be dealt with in a detached and dispassionate way with a view only to what is best for Canada. That is the policy I propose to pursue. So long as this government is in power the immigration policy of this country will never again be dictated by transportation companies and booking agencies and those who have very little else but their own material interest at heart.

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to hear the statement the minister has made. I discovered, however, in the reading room what purports to be a reproduction of an advertisement which appeared in the old country papers. It reads as follows:
Canada

Call and discuss it with the Canadian government representative.
